A retired judge sitting as a referee under the lease's dispute resolution clause tried the case over five days in January 2024 and found that Pacific never had the funds or loan commitments to close, had been stalling, and was in material breach of a lease that made time of the essence. The trial court entered judgment for the defendants on May 28, 2024. On appeal, the Second District accepted that the lease's reference to acquiring title under the purchase agreement could be read to tie Pacific's deadline to the ExxonMobil contract, but refused to let that reading give Pacific unlimited control over its own performance. Applying Civil Code section 1657 and the implied covenant of good faith, the panel held that Pacific had to close within a reasonable time. It found ample support for the referee's conclusion that Pacific's delay was unreasonable, pointing to the option terms that contemplated a 2019 closing and to testimony that the delay was a deliberate cost-saving choice. The court also rejected Pacific's argument that its duty to buy the land was excused until TGS obtained its cannabis license. Nothing in the lease made the purchase conditional on licensing, while a separate clause expressly deferred construction until permits issued, which the panel read as showing the parties knew how to write such a condition when they wanted one. The court called the risk of buying land before licensing the deal Pacific struck. The judgment for TGS and Jushi was affirmed and they were awarded appellate costs. The opinion is unpublished; an order filed October 13 corrected only the trial court case number. For developers, the practical point is to put a firm acquisition deadline, financing contingency or licensing condition in writing in any lease signed before closing on the land, rather than relying on a pending purchase contract. Tenants and guarantors, for their part, can use the reasonable-time rule to exit a deal when a landlord's delay goes to the heart of the bargain, provided they document repeated requests to perform, as TGS did here.
live-280: Ordinary Faces LLC leased space from Bohemian Brethren Presbyterian Church to operate a preschool in a New York City building. To run the school, the tenant needed a letter of no objection from the city Department of Buildings. The Department initially refused because the building lacked a working fire alarm system, and the Fire Department did not sign off on an alarm until July 26, 2016, nearly two years after the lease was signed. Open Department of Buildings violations tied to a defunct dumbwaiter shaft, in a part of the building outside the leased premises, also stood in the way of a permanent letter. The tenant and its founder sued the church in New York County Supreme Court in 2017. After a jury trial before Justice Joel M. Cohen, judgment was entered on August 20, 2025 awarding the plaintiffs $1,216,177.36. The church appealed the judgment and several pretrial and post-trial rulings, including the denial of its motion to set aside the verdict and its motion to strike the jury demand. The First Department found the evidence sufficient. It held that the church breached section 18(a) of the lease, which required it to cooperate in obtaining approvals for the school, by never having its elevator company file the paperwork needed to clear the violations, and breached a lease rider requiring both sides to move expeditiously and diligently on the fire alarm. Because the violations were issued against areas the tenant did not lease, the court said curing them was the landlord's job. A church officer's own testimony that the requested filing was never made helped seal the point. The panel rejected the church's argument that a 50 percent rent abatement from January through August 2015 was the tenant's sole remedy, noting that the rider did not say so. It also upheld the lost-profits portion of the award, $734,353, or roughly two and a half years of projected profits. The tenant had built its figures from operating data for a preschool that had occupied the same space for nearly 40 years, data the church itself supplied, and its first-year results matched its projections; the church offered no contrary evidence. Two lease defenses also failed. Section 19 limited the tenant to the landlord's estate and interest in the building and its rents, but the court held that language allows recovery from the proceeds of the church's 2019 sale of the building, and the church offered no proof the award exceeded its sale profits. The church's reliance on the lease's jury waivers came four months after the note of issue and after its counsel had told the court there was no dispute about a jury, so the trial court properly found the waiver itself had been waived. The court also declined to order a new trial over brief, unsolicited testimony about the founder's personal history, which the church had not objected to at trial. For landlords, the decision is a reminder that cooperation and diligence clauses in leases to schools, medical users and other permit-dependent tenants carry real damages exposure, especially for violations in common or non-demised areas only the owner can cure. Owners who want abatement to be an exclusive remedy, or who want to keep a jury waiver, need to say so expressly and enforce it early. Tenants should document the owner's specific failures to file or cure, as this tenant did.
live-281: Recycled Properties, LLC operates a construction and demolition debris landfill and borrow pit in Chesapeake, Virginia, uses that are legally nonconforming under the city's current zoning. In May 2024 it submitted a site plan to the city's Department of Development and Permits to put up a warehouse and an office building on the property. In August 2024 the city disapproved the plan, reasoning that the buildings would expand the nonconforming use, that it lacked enough information about how the buildings would be used, and that a conditional use permit for the nonconforming operations would be needed before approval. The city also cited past zoning violations, a ground it later withdrew. The owner appealed to the Chesapeake Circuit Court under the Virginia statutes that let an applicant challenge a site plan disapproval as unsupported by the ordinance or arbitrary and capricious. It argued that the zoning ordinance did not require it to prove the buildings were not an expansion, did not authorize a demand for more information, and did not allow the city to require a conditional use permit for existing operations. It separately sought damages under a state statute addressing unconstitutional conditions on land use approvals. The city demurred, and the circuit court sustained the demurrer while noting the owner could file a new site plan. In a memorandum opinion by Judge Kevin M. Duffan, the Court of Appeals affirmed. The panel pointed to the city's denial letter, which the owner had attached to its own complaint. That letter relied on a Chesapeake ordinance provision barring additional buildings or structures that support a lawfully nonconforming use and on the city's authority to review site plans for conformity with the zoning ordinance. The court cited Virginia Supreme Court precedent allowing localities to prohibit expansion of nonconforming uses. Because nothing in the complaint factually disputed that the buildings would alter or expand the nonconforming use, or that more information was needed, the court treated the owner's contrary assertions as legal conclusions that a court need not accept on demurrer. It held the circuit court applied the correct pleading standard rather than deciding the merits on a summary judgment basis, as the owner claimed. The owner's argument that the denial was unconstitutional was not reached because it was not raised in an assignment of error on appeal. The opinion is unpublished. For owners and developers of industrial, salvage, landfill and other grandfathered properties, the case underlines that even ancillary improvements such as an office or storage building can be treated as an expansion of a nonconforming use. Before filing a site plan, owners should be ready to document that new structures will not intensify or extend the existing use, or plan for a conditional use permit or rezoning. If a denial is appealed, the complaint should plead specific facts that answer each ground in the denial letter rather than rest on legal argument.
live-282: In December 2023 the City of Bradford, Pennsylvania filed a declaration of taking to condemn 374 square feet of an alley running through the rear of a property owned by DewBoi Properties, LLC, as part of a project to build a new bus station. DewBoi filed preliminary objections, and the parties' lawyers negotiated a settlement over several months in 2024. In October 2024 DewBoi's counsel accepted the city's offer of $30,000 plus the removal and relocation of two telephone poles at the city's expense. The city's draft agreement of sale said the poles would be moved out of the alley to DewBoi's property. DewBoi's counsel revised a related joint stipulation to drop the express reference to DewBoi's property but left the agreement of sale language unchanged, and the city accepted the revisions. The city signed in December 2024, the parties told the court they had settled, and DewBoi's counsel received the city's $30,000 check on January 6, 2025. The deal unraveled when the city sent over the local electric utility's easement, which showed one pole moving to another spot on DewBoi's lot. DewBoi objected that the proposed locations would further cut into parking for its tenants and their customers. After the city began building the bus station and put up a temporary fence across the condemned strip, affecting access to DewBoi's parking lot, DewBoi sought a preliminary injunction in May 2025, arguing the city did not own the land. The city responded with a petition to enforce the settlement. After two days of hearings, the McKean County Court of Common Pleas granted the city's petition and denied the injunction on August 25, 2025. On appeal, DewBoi argued there was no meeting of the minds on where the poles would go and, at most, a mutual mistake. In a non-precedential memorandum opinion by Judge Lori A. Dumas, the Commonwealth Court disagreed. It held that the settlement documents, read together, clearly provided for relocating both poles from the alley to other places on DewBoi's property. It also deferred to the trial court's findings, based on months of correspondence, the city attorney's testimony, the joint report of settlement and DewBoi's request for the $30,000 check, that the owner had approved the deal and later had second thoughts about vehicle access. Without clear, precise and convincing proof of a shared mistaken assumption, the mutual mistake defense failed. The case is small in dollars but common in practice. Commercial owners facing partial takings for transit, road or utility projects should treat site-plan details such as pole, sign, curb cut and parking locations as material terms, attach drawings to the settlement, and confirm the utility's easement before signing. Once a settlement is signed, reported to the court and funded, Pennsylvania courts are likely to enforce it as written.
live-283: ApplianceSmart, Inc. operated a store in the big-box space of a Columbus, Ohio shopping center owned by Trustees Main/270, LLC from 2008 to 2022. The lease began with a predecessor entity, Appliance Recycling Centers of America, which became the guarantor in 2017 when ApplianceSmart took over as tenant and the term was extended to June 30, 2025. That guarantor was later reincorporated as JanOne, Inc. and stayed on the guaranty after JanOne sold ApplianceSmart to Live Ventures, Inc. in 2019. According to the opinion, the tenant defaulted three times. A 2019 rent default ended in a settlement of a state-court suit. A second default during ApplianceSmart's 2021 bankruptcy was resolved with an amendment under which Live Ventures agreed to pay more than $185,000 in back rent, and the landlord gained a new one-sided right to terminate on 30 days' notice. After a third payment default in February 2022, the landlord used a lease clause that let it retake possession and change the locks without ending the lease, leaving the tenant responsible for rent and reletting costs. It then sued ApplianceSmart and JanOne for breach of the lease and the guaranty. The defendants did not dispute that they had breached. Their defense was mitigation. The guarantor proposed an affiliated recycling business that would assume the existing lease and keep trading under the ApplianceSmart name, and Live Ventures offered one of its own portfolio companies, a flooring retailer. The landlord asked the first candidate to prepay all arrears and post a nonrefundable six-month deposit, which JanOne refused. It sent the second candidate a standard questionnaire, which went unanswered. The landlord's broker kept marketing the space, and AutoZone signed a lease in September 2024. Because of zoning and permitting contingencies, AutoZone did not begin paying rent until after the ApplianceSmart term would have ended. The district court awarded the undisputed back rent on summary judgment and held a bench trial on mitigation, finding the landlord's efforts reasonable. In an opinion that is not recommended for publication, the Sixth Circuit affirmed. Applying the Ohio Supreme Court's decision in Frenchtown Square Partnership v. Lemstone and the Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 350, the panel said a commercial lessor must make reasonable efforts to relet but need not accept just any available tenant, and need not take on undue risk. Both proposed replacements shared ownership or key decision-makers with the parties behind the three defaults, so rejecting them, or demanding protective terms, was reasonable. The panel also rejected an analogy to employment-law cases about unconditional job offers, and found the argument about a rejected purchase offer likely forfeited, noting that Ohio landlords are not required to sell the building to mitigate. Before reaching the merits, the panel raised on its own that the complaint had not properly alleged the citizenship of the parties, including the landlord LLC's members. It accepted supplemental letter briefs that traced the landlord's membership through partnerships and trusts to Ohio and Florida citizens, and treated them as amendments under 28 U.S.C. section 1653 to confirm diversity jurisdiction. For landlords, the practical lesson is to document the re-leasing process: broker outreach, why each candidate was accepted or declined, and the credit concerns behind any conditions. A tenant's or guarantor's affiliate is not owed an easy path back into the space. Tenants and guarantors who want to cap their exposure through a substitute tenant should offer real credit support and full financial disclosure. Counsel filing diversity suits for LLC or trust-owned landlords should plead each member's citizenship in full from the start.
live-284: The dispute concerns a 117-bed assisted-living facility built on land in Conroe, Texas. The property-owning company, Conroe WM LLC, financed construction with a loan from Greystone Funding Company LLC, insured by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development under its Section 232 program for residential care facilities. HUD required the borrower to fund several escrows: working capital, minor movable equipment and an initial operating deficit. HREF Senior Worthington LLC, which once operated under a MidHudson name, came into the deal in 2019 to fund them. HREF put $4.5 million into WM Conroe Property Holdings LLC, the holding company that manages the property owner. About $3.24 million covered the HUD escrows. The other $1.27 million funded the first 25 months of HREF's monthly return. HREF took special membership interests rather than common equity or management rights. In exchange, it bargained for the right to become the holding company's sole manager immediately if it was not paid. The redemption date was later extended to August 2024, and the monthly payment was raised to $40,000. According to the Chancery opinion, payments stopped after February 2024. HREF declared its step-in right in November 2024 and sued in the Court of Chancery that month. One count sought a summary declaration under 6 Del. C. Section 18-110 that HREF was now the holding company's sole manager. That count was tried on a paper record in August 2025. The defendants were the property owner and WM Property Holdings LLC, the sponsor-side manager. They argued that the HUD documents and the property owner's operating agreement barred any change in management without HUD's prior written approval. They also argued that HREF's step-in addendum was illegal and that HUD had to be part of the case. In a January 12, 2026 memorandum opinion, the Court of Chancery rejected each argument. It held that the HUD approval provisions bound the property-owning borrower, not the holding company above it. It also held that the HUD documents did not control who could manage the holding company, that the HREF addendum was not illegal, and that the parties before the court were enough to resolve the control dispute. The court ruled that HREF was entitled to become the holding company's sole manager immediately. It held HREF's fee request in abeyance while the remaining claims proceed. The defendants appealed. After briefing and oral argument, the Delaware Supreme Court affirmed by order on October 8, 2026, adopting the Court of Chancery's reasoning. The panel was the Chief Justice and two Justices. The other counts in HREF's amended complaint are still pending in the Court of Chancery. For investors in HUD-financed senior housing and similar regulated deals, the practical point is to place step-in and removal rights at a holding company that sits outside the HUD-regulated borrower. The agreements should say clearly which entity owes the payments and what default triggers the takeover. Sponsors should assume that pointing to agency approval rules written for the borrower will not stop an upstream investor from taking control once its own triggers are met. Lenders and investors should still plan for HUD notice and approval steps at the property level after they take over the holding company.
live-285: Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg County, a local group represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center, sued Spartanburg County in July 2026. The suit challenged how the county was handling permits for a data center campus being built by Valara Holdings, which South Carolina Lawyers Weekly describes as a subsidiary of NorthMark Cloud and Compute. The project is planned on South Pine Street, at the site of the old Kohler plant. It is reported as a $2.8 billion investment. SELC's filing materials describe about 500,000 square feet of new buildings, a power yard, internal roads and a 450-megawatt gas-fired power plant. The suit rested on the county's Unified Land Management Ordinance. The group argued that Valara had applied for, and county staff were processing, a 'minor' land development permit, which gets staff-only review with no public hearing. In the group's view a project of this size met the ordinance's definition of a 'major' development. That would have required review by the Planning Commission, plus public notice and comment. The complaint asked for a declaration that the county must require a major development permit, and for an injunction stopping the county from processing the minor application. The first permit, for redeveloping the Kohler building, was approved in August 2025. A second application, covering four new buildings, the power yard and cooling systems, is still pending. Judge J. Derham Cole Jr. dismissed the case on October 6 and did not decide whether the project was correctly classified. Local coverage reports two grounds. First, standing: under South Carolina law, neighbors who want to block a project must show they were specially damaged. The court found the group's concerns about noise, dust, traffic, health and transparency too general to meet that test. Second, exhaustion: county rules give an appeal to the Board of Zoning Appeals, reportedly with a 10-day filing window, and the group had not used it. As for the second permit, the court said a challenge was premature because the county has not yet acted on it. A hearing on the group's request to pause construction had been held on September 17, and the dismissal ends that request. SELC says the ruling conflicts with South Carolina Supreme Court precedent. It argues that residents could not have used the zoning-appeal route because the project was not described as a data center when it was permitted, and it expects to file a notice of appeal. The fight goes beyond zoning. SELC is pressing a separate challenge before the South Carolina Court of Appeals over whether Valara needed Public Service Commission approval. It has also asked state environmental regulators to reopen comment on the project's air permit, which the state issued in September, over formaldehyde emissions from the planned gas turbines. Spartanburg County separately paused new data center applications for one year in June 2026. Coverage notes that the pause does not reach Valara, because its project was already underway. In practical terms, the decision is a clear example of procedural defenses deciding a land-use case before the merits are reached. Developers that move through staff-level approvals can gain a lot when neighbors miss short administrative appeal deadlines. They should still expect opponents to try every other forum available, including utility regulators, air permits and appeals. Owners repurposing former manufacturing plants for data centers should document the basis for their permit classification from the start, because that classification is now a common target. Lenders and investors should treat a trial-court standing win as an interim result while an appeal and parallel regulatory challenges are pending.
live-286: Hetley Associates owns Hetley Plaza, a strip shopping center in Lemoyne Borough, Cumberland County, zoned Commercial General. It also owns three nearby residential lots in the borough's Urban Residential District, one of them a rented house. The center operates as a lawful nonconforming use with fewer parking spaces than the ordinance now requires. The owner argued that changing conditions around the plaza had made the shortage worse, and that a vacant space once occupied by a restaurant was hard to re-lease without more parking. In January 2025 the owner asked the borough Zoning Hearing Board for a use variance to demolish the three houses and pave a parking lot in their place. After a hearing, the Board denied the request on March 27, 2025. Among other reasons, it found that the owner's own decision to lease to a restaurant had added to the parking problem. The Court of Common Pleas of Cumberland County affirmed on September 4, 2025, after argument in August. It found that the residential lots could keep being used as rentals, for which there is demand, and that the hardship the owner described related to the plaza rather than to the lots in question. On appeal, the owner challenged each of the Board's findings: that the variance would change the character of the neighborhood, that the hardship was self-created, that following the ordinance was practical, and that the request was not the minimum variance needed. In a memorandum opinion filed October 9, 2026, the Commonwealth Court affirmed on a single ground and did not reach the others. Both the borough ordinance and the Municipalities Planning Code require unnecessary hardship arising from physical conditions unique to the property for which relief is sought. Relying on its earlier decision in Bawa Muhaiyaddeen Fellowship, the court explained that the hardship must belong to the property, not to the person who owns it. Applying that rule, the court found that the owner was really claiming a hardship to its commercial plaza: it could not expand that use without taking over the neighboring residential land. Because the residential lots stay usable and valuable for their permitted residential use, there was no unnecessary hardship tied to them. The court noted that the owner cited no authority allowing a variance on one property based on hardship to another. In a footnote, the court also rejected the owner's suggestion that the minimum-variance requirement does not apply to use variances, pointing to its own decisions holding that it does. The court added that, although one owner holds both the plaza and the residential lots, they remain separate parcels, and nothing in the record showed an attempt to combine them. It expressly declined to say whether a reverse subdivision would have been proper or would change the result. The opinion is labeled non-precedential, so it can be cited as persuasive authority but is not binding in Pennsylvania. For retail landlords, the practical lesson is that parking shortfalls at older centers usually cannot be solved by buying adjoining residential lots and asking for a use variance. Better options include a rezoning or text amendment, a parking-reduction or shared-parking provision, an off-site parking agreement on commercially zoned land, or, where the ordinance allows, combining parcels before applying, though the court left that last route open rather than endorsing it. Owners should also expect a zoning board to count leasing decisions, such as bringing in a parking-heavy restaurant tenant, as a self-created hardship. Buyers and lenders evaluating a nonconforming center should treat any planned parking expansion that depends on a variance as uncertain.
live-287: San Francisco Care Center, L.P. borrowed up to $23,108,000 in 2002 from Pacific Commonwealth Mortgage Company to build a senior health care facility in San Francisco. It began operating the property as an assisted-living facility for elderly and memory-care residents in 2004. The loan was assigned to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development in May 2006, and HUD sold it to Lenox Mortgage IX LLC that December. The bankruptcy court later called the loan documents "terribly outdated and nothing like what is routinely seen today." The borrower first defaulted around 2006 or 2007 and cured it in 2008 by paying $252,470.56, a figure that included no attorneys' fees. It then sued Lenox in state court to force the release of more construction funds, and later dismissed that suit voluntarily. Years later, legal costs from a building-code suit brought by the City of San Francisco, which the operator won in 2023, combined with the pandemic to strain its finances. It stopped making loan payments in early 2024. Lenox recorded a notice of default in September 2024 and set a foreclosure sale for January 14, 2025. The operator filed Chapter 11 that same day. Lenox filed a proof of claim for $19,189,226.25. In May 2025 the bankruptcy court approved a section 363 sale of the property for $27,750,000 in cash. Under the sale order, any challenged part of a payoff demand was held in escrow. Lenox's demand was $19,822,204.53, plus per diem interest, $1,910,657.89 in unpaid interest and $419,266.94 in attorneys' fees. Lenox broke the fees down as $187,324.54 for the first default, $139,035.94 for the state-court suit, $56,073.32 for the second default and $87,162 for the bankruptcy and payoff litigation. Judge Dennis Montali disallowed all of the fees. In a December 1, 2025 order he also granted the debtor its own fees and costs under California Civil Code section 1717. The case was converted to Chapter 7 in April 2026. The panel read the note, deed of trust and security agreement closely. The note allowed only fees that a court adjudged reasonable in an action on the note, and no court ever did that. The deed of trust covered actions affecting Lenox's security, but the construction-funds suit did not threaten the lien. The nonjudicial notices of default were also not court proceedings. The security agreement allowed fees only out of foreclosure-sale proceeds, and the property was sold through the bankruptcy court rather than at foreclosure. The panel ruled the other way on the bankruptcy-related fees. Lenox had appeared in the case to protect its lien, through the cash-collateral order, its proof of claim and its objections to the sale order. The panel also held that the payoff litigation could not be an action on the contract for the borrower's section 1717 fee claim and yet not an action for Lenox's own fee recovery. It reversed on those fees and sent the case back for a reasonableness determination. It also vacated the borrower's fee award so the bankruptcy court can decide who now counts as the prevailing party. For lenders buying seasoned or agency-originated loans, the practical lesson is to check the fee clauses before relying on the right to add legal costs to the debt. Narrow clauses tied to court awards or foreclosure proceeds may not survive a bankruptcy sale. Lenders should ask a court to award fees when litigation is pending instead of quietly accruing them, and should weigh the risk of a reciprocal fee award under section 1717 before contesting a payoff. Borrowers and buyers in distressed senior-living and other single-asset sales should read the old loan documents with equal care, because the escrow holdback for disputed charges can be released.
live-288: Enterprise Bank and Trust held the first deed of trust on ten Laguna Beach, California parcels. Each parcel was owned by its own single-asset real estate entity, including Laguna Festival Center, LLC, Laguna Art District Complex, LLC, 891 Laguna Canyon Road, LLC, 694 NCH Apartments, LLC and Duplex at Sleepy Hollow, LLC. The properties had a collective book value of about $95 million, and Enterprise was owed roughly $80 million. Each parcel carried at least three deeds of trust. The owners had stopped paying property taxes and regular loan payments. Enterprise sent a default notice in November 2024 and recorded notices of default in February 2025. The defaults came against the backdrop of a long-running dispute over control of the ownership entities. Within three weeks of the default notices, the owners and twelve affiliates filed voluntary Chapter 11 cases in Delaware, jointly administered under MOM CA Investco LLC. Enterprise obtained unopposed stay relief on July 15, 2025, and the Delaware cases were dismissed in August 2025. Enterprise then sued in California state court, which appointed a receiver over the properties on October 7, 2025. Enterprise also noticed nonjudicial foreclosure sales for 3:00 p.m. on October 15, 2025. On the afternoon of the sales, between 2:28 and 3:02 p.m., creditors including Vierergruppe Management, Inc. filed involuntary Chapter 11 petitions against all ten owners in Santa Ana. Neither Enterprise nor the foreclosure trustee knew. The sales ran from 3:13 to 3:52 p.m. About twenty unrelated people attended, but only one outside bid was placed, on the 694 NCH property. That sale was later canceled and the money returned. Enterprise took the other nine properties by credit bid. The owners opposed stay relief by offering a $102 million purchase agreement with Special Assets Laguna, LLC. Bankruptcy Judge Scott C. Clarkson found the involuntary cases were filed in bad faith. In December 2025 he granted Enterprise prospective and in rem relief and retroactively annulled the stay as to the nine properties without outside bids, which validated those sales. He ordered the petitioning creditors to post a $1 million bond. They did not, and the ten cases were dismissed on March 18, 2026. The owners dropped their own appeals in June 2026, which left only the appeal of a prospective bidder. That bidder said he held back because he had heard of the filings, and argued that the petitions chilled the bidding. The panel first held that the appeal was not moot and that the bidder had standing, because he had changed his conduct in reliance on the stay. On the merits, it held that the equities analysis under the Fjeldsted factors properly looked at the debtors' bad faith, the lender's lack of notice, its earlier stay relief and how quickly it moved, and not only at the bidder's position. It noted that the bidder had not alerted the trustee or placed a bid. It also found nothing inconsistent in treating the rescinded 694 NCH sale differently, because that property is the subject of a separate appeal. For lenders, the decision supports moving quickly to annul the stay when related parties file a bankruptcy at the last minute, particularly after an earlier case produced stay relief. For borrowers and their affiliates, serial or involuntary filings timed to the auction risk bad-faith findings, bond requirements and dismissal. For investors who bid at foreclosure sales, the safer course when a bankruptcy is rumored is to tell the trustee or bid anyway. Waiting quietly may leave no remedy if the sale is later validated.
live-289: Braemar Hotels & Resorts Inc., a NYSE-listed REIT based in Dallas that owns luxury hotels and resorts, has settled a wide-ranging dispute with its largest stockholder, Al Shams Investments Limited, a Bermuda company. The Cooperation and Settlement Agreement is dated October 6, 2026. Its other signatories are Ashford Hospitality Trust, Inc. and Ashford Inc., and the beneficial owner of Al Shams signed for limited purposes. Braemar filed the agreement as an exhibit to a Form 8-K on October 8, 2026. A company press release that day announced it alongside a portfolio update and the pending $372 million sale of the Four Seasons Resort Scottsdale. The agreement's recitals set out what was being resolved. Al Shams had sent Braemar a notice nominating a slate of director candidates for the 2026 annual meeting. It had also asserted or threatened direct claims against the company group, including defamation and libel claims, claims under the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and claims similar to those earlier brought by another investor and Morning View Hotels BH1, LLC. Separately, it had asserted or threatened derivative claims on Braemar's behalf alleging fiduciary breaches by the board and management. Al Shams was also pursuing a verified petition under Texas Rule of Civil Procedure 202 to depose two former Braemar directors before filing suit. The company group denies wrongdoing, and no party admits liability. The money terms are substantial. Braemar agreed to pay Al Shams $25 million for the settlement and releases, plus $15 million to reimburse expenses Al Shams incurred in the conflict. That is $40 million in total, payable as $20 million on signing and $10 million each at four and eight months. Each installment depends on Al Shams continuing to comply. Disputes over a claimed breach go to expedited JAMS arbitration in Dallas, and a final finding of material breach triggers a clawback of everything paid. If cash is short, Braemar may pay up to $4 million of the later installments in common stock, and the board must grant an exception to the REIT's 9.8% ownership limit if that issuance would push Al Shams over the cap. Al Shams also gave up a great deal. It withdrew its nominations and the Rule 202 petition and agreed to a 10-year standstill. Under the standstill it may not run proxy contests, join groups, buy more shares, comment on extraordinary transactions, short the stock, or bring any litigation or pre-suit discovery against the companies or their current and former directors and officers, except to enforce the agreement. It must vote with the board's recommendations, and it waived any right to share in other stockholders' derivative or class recoveries. In return, Al Shams may consult with Braemar's director search firm on candidates for one board seat, but the board keeps sole discretion over the choice. Both sides exchanged general releases and agreed not to disparage each other. Braemar's 8-K describes the headline figure as $25 million plus expenses. The company expects its own net contribution to be only $4 million to $6 million after insurance proceeds and Ashford's share. Under a separate Allocation Agreement, Braemar and Ashford each bear half of the payments net of insurance, which both are pursuing, although Braemar cautions that the insurance recovery is not assured. The company says the settlement likely costs less than the litigation it avoided. The 2026 annual meeting is set for December 21, 2026, and the press release says the separation from Ashford should be finished by mid-November. There are several lessons here for REIT boards, external advisors and their D&O carriers. First, Texas Rule 202 petitions can be used as leverage before any suit is filed, and a REIT based in Texas should expect activists to use them to depose former directors. Second, once an activist with a large stake combines a proxy contest with securities, derivative and defamation claims, the case can be settled at a figure far above ordinary expense reimbursement. Paying in installments with a clawback, as here, protects the company if the activist later breaks its promises. Third, splitting costs with the external advisor and leaning on insurance can bring the REIT's net cost far below the gross number. Investors should watch whether the second and third installments are paid in cash or stock, and whether the insurers actually pay.
live-290: The Michigan Court of Appeals on October 13, 2026 affirmed a trial court ruling that handed Grant Township, a local government in Grand Traverse County, a decisive win over a commercial landowner that had sought to force a public hearing on its special land use application. The unpublished, per curiam decision in Schell Road, LLC v. Vanderford rejected developer Schell Road, LLC's bid for a writ of mandamus against the township's zoning administrator and planning commission, and upheld the township's decision to amend its mining ordinance while the litigation was pending. Schell Road, LLC purchased 80 acres on Schell Road in Grant Township in 2022, intending to develop and operate a gravel mine. The company submitted an initial special land use application that September, with site plans from a civil engineer. It was the first mining-operation application the township had received since 2003, and it prompted officials to question whether the township's zoning ordinance, unchanged on mining regulations since 1998, properly accounted for state law that had been amended in 2011. While the township studied that question, Schell Road submitted supplemental materials in December 2022 and January 2023 to address what officials described as deficiencies in the original filing, and township officials told the company they intended to delay consideration of the application until the ordinance could be amended. After an exchange of letters in which Schell Road's counsel accused the township of deliberately delaying review, the company filed a circuit court complaint in February 2023 seeking a writ of mandamus to compel a public hearing. While that case was pending, the Grant Township Planning Commission recommended, and the township board adopted, amendments to the mining provisions of the zoning ordinance, effective March 30, 2023. Schell Road amended its complaint to add claims that the amendments were enacted in bad faith specifically to block its application, along with due process, injunctive and declaratory-relief theories. The Grand Traverse Circuit Court sided with the township on cross-motions for summary disposition, finding that Schell Road's original application was incomplete under the township's own pre-amendment ordinance and that the company therefore never had the clear, legal right to a hearing that mandamus relief requires in Michigan. The trial court also rejected the bad-faith theory, concluding the amended ordinance complied with the state statute governing township zoning, MCL 125.3205. On appeal, a panel of Judges Korobkin, Rick and Maldonado affirmed across the board. The court held that whether an application is complete under a zoning ordinance can be resolved as a question of law on summary disposition rather than left to a jury, and that the trial court was entitled to weigh the documentary record, including the parties' correspondence and the civil engineer's site plans, in reaching that conclusion. Because Schell Road could not establish the clear legal right mandamus requires, the panel did not need to disturb the trial court's separate finding that the ordinance amendment itself was not adopted in bad faith. The case is a reminder to commercial developers and their counsel that a mandamus claim against a local government lives or dies on the completeness of the underlying application measured against the ordinance as it existed when filed, and that courts will treat that as a legal question they can decide without a trial once the record is developed. It also confirms that a municipality retains real latitude to amend its own zoning ordinance while a litigant's case is pending, particularly where it can point to an independent, long-standing rationale, here an ordinance unrevised for roughly a quarter-century against a statutory backdrop that had already changed, and that absent a strong, record-supported showing that the amendment targeted one applicant's project, courts are unlikely to second-guess its timing. Developers chasing a special land use permit for mining or similar extractive uses should build a complete, well-documented application record from the outset rather than relying on the pendency of litigation to freeze the regulatory landscape in their favor.
live-291: C&B Development, LLC is the equitable owner, under a 2022 purchase agreement, of a 75.5-acre tract in Maxatawny Township, Berks County. The site now holds a restaurant, a mobile home park and an airport. The tract is split among three zoning districts: Commercial (C-1), Light Industrial (L-I) and Agricultural Preservation (AP-1). Its only street frontage is on Kutztown Road. The developer planned to clear the site and build a commercial building plus a 709,000-square-foot warehouse on the L-I portion. That portion can be reached only by a new private drive, called Road A in the record, running from Kutztown Road through the commercial district. The problem was an October 2022 ordinance amendment. It made warehouses and distribution facilities a conditional use in the L-I district, rather than a use permitted by right, and added Section 593(c). That section requires warehouse buildings and all related impervious surfaces to sit at least 500 feet from any building occupied by an existing residential, institutional or educational use. In August 2023 the township's zoning officer found that Road A was an impervious surface serving the warehouse. Because the road could not be routed 500 feet away from nearby homes, it did not comply. He told the developer to get a variance before its conditional use hearing could go forward. The developer appealed to the Zoning Hearing Board. It argued that the road was not covered by the buffer rule and, in the alternative, asked for a dimensional variance. After three hearings ending in January 2024, the board sided with the zoning officer and denied the variance. The board found that the property could support many other permitted uses that do not carry the 500-foot buffer. It also found that routing truck traffic onto Kutztown Road would harm a largely residential area that Kutztown University students use. The Berks County Court of Common Pleas affirmed on July 14, 2025, and the developer appealed. In a memorandum opinion by Judge Patricia A. McCullough, the Commonwealth Court rejected all three of the developer's arguments. First, the zoning officer did not testify, but that was no ground for reversal. The board has its own authority to interpret the ordinance, and the developer had the chance to subpoena him and dropped it. Second, the conditional use provision and the buffer rule do not conflict, so the rule in the Municipalities Planning Code that resolves doubtful ordinance language in the owner's favor did not apply. Third, the board applied the correct variance test. The developer's own brief admitted that the light-industrial lot could be used for things other than a warehouse, so its hardship was self-imposed and not caused by the property. The panel also noted that the developer never filed a formal challenge to the ordinance's validity, which is the proper route for an argument that the zoning leaves no reasonable use. The opinion notes that the developer has a separate inverse condemnation suit pending against the township in the Berks County court. In that suit it alleges a coordinated effort to block the project. The appellate court refused to consider any of that record in the land use appeal. The decision is unreported and non-precedential. It ends this zoning route unless the developer seeks further review, but it does not resolve the separate takings claim. The practical lesson is that local warehouse ordinances increasingly measure setbacks from all related paving, not just from the building, and access drives count. A buyer should map every required road, drive and loading area against residential and institutional buffers during due diligence, especially on sites with one frontage. A variance request based on the inability to build one preferred use is unlikely to succeed when the district allows other uses. A developer who believes an ordinance leaves no reasonable use of the land must bring a formal validity challenge under the Municipalities Planning Code. That argument cannot be raised for the first time in a variance appeal.
live-292: 865 East 49th Street Associates LLC, a commercial landlord, sued its tenant Valdo Auto Sales Corp. and others in Miami-Dade County Circuit Court (Lower Tribunal No. 22-17871-CA-01). The trial court, Judge Valerie R. Manno Schurr presiding, entered summary judgment orders on liability and damages in the landlord's favor. Liability was resolved by an order titled "Agreed Summary Final Judgment as to Liability," which covered all of the landlord's claims, including fraud and unjust enrichment. The only money awarded, however, was $76,199.37 in past-due rent for breach of the commercial lease. The landlord appealed, arguing that once liability was established on the fraud and unjust enrichment counts, the trial court could not award zero dollars on them. The tenant did not appear in the appeal. A panel of Judges Fernandez, Gordo and Rebull heard the case, and Judge Gordo wrote the opinion affirming the trial court. The court started from the rule against double recovery. A plaintiff who wins a contract award must show that its fraud or unjust enrichment damages are separate and distinct from that award, and not just the same loss counted again. Fraud requires actual damages as an essential element, and a liability finding alone does not establish them. Unjust enrichment requires competent, quantified evidence of the value of the benefit conferred. The panel cited Florida cases holding that a plaintiff can win liability and still recover nothing. Procedure also decided the appeal. The trial court resolved liability, damages and rehearing only after full in-court hearings, but the landlord did not supply a transcript of any of them or an approved statement of the evidence. Because the liability judgment was an agreed order, nothing in the record showed what the parties had agreed to. In particular, the record did not show whether the landlord kept or gave up any claim to separate damages. The panel would not assume that the agreed judgment decided more than the liability it recites. It found no genuine issue of material fact on any compensable, non-duplicative damages and affirmed. The opinion is not final until any timely rehearing motion is resolved. There are several lessons for commercial landlords and their lawyers. First, fraud and unjust enrichment counts in a rent case need their own damages proof, with a dollar figure tied to a loss the lease award does not already cover. Second, an agreed liability judgment should say expressly whether damages on each claim are reserved for later decision. Third, if a summary judgment or damages hearing may be appealed, have a court reporter there. Without a transcript, Florida appellate courts will generally presume the trial court's ruling was correct.
live-293: Valley Post is a four-building dining and entertainment development off Dunnavant Valley Road in Chelsea, Alabama, in Shelby County south of Birmingham. A Birmingham developer built it, and its only operator was a Pihakis Restaurant Group affiliate. It housed four concepts: Hero Diner, Luca & Lucy, Little Donkey and Rodney Scott BBQ. According to court documents described by AL.com, the development opened in December 2025, and no rent was paid from that month on. In April 2026 the Pihakis Restaurant Group began closing more than a dozen restaurants in four states, and all four Valley Post restaurants shut at once. That month the landlord side filed liens on several properties leased to the group and its affiliates. WBRC reported that the amended Valley Post lien, filed April 27, claimed $7,166,296.20 plus attorney fees and other expenses for rent due under the leases. In June, the landlord entity, Dunnavant Valley Dining LLC, sued in Shelby County Circuit Court. It alleged that PRG Valley Post had defaulted on a long-term lease of the four buildings, with charges totaling about $7.35 million. The tenant never answered, and the court entered a default judgment for $7.19 million in unpaid rent, attorney fees and court costs, as AL.com reported on October 7, 2026. According to that report, the court certified the judgment as final, which makes it immediately enforceable, and post-judgment interest accrues until it is paid. How the judgment will be collected is unclear. The defendant is a project-level operating affiliate of a restaurant group that has largely shut down. The landlord has already re-tenanted part of the property: Waldo's Chicken and Beer opened a Valley Post location on September 29, and Saw's BBQ is expected to open there later this fall. Rent collected from replacement tenants could affect how much the landlord can ultimately recover for the same period. Published reporting does not say whether the leases carried guaranties or how the award was calculated against the roughly $7.35 million originally claimed. For landlords and developers, Valley Post is a warning about a common structure in restaurant-anchored projects: the whole development leased to one operator through a newly formed affiliate. A default judgment against that affiliate can be quick and large, but it is only worth what the affiliate owns. Owners leasing to restaurant groups should make sure guaranties come from an entity with real assets. They should also watch rent from opening day, because here no rent was paid from the start, and record liens or seek security early. Leases should be drafted so the space can be relet quickly without giving up the claim for the remaining term.
live-294: The Massachusetts Appeals Court reversed a Land Court judgment on October 14, 2026 that had declared CRG Acquisition, LLC's proposed 800,000-square-foot warehouse and distribution facility in Holliston a use permitted as of right, meaning no special permit was required. The panel's ruling effectively reinstates the position of the town and its planning board, which had already denied CRG a special permit for the project in 2021 after eleven public hearings. Because that discretionary denial was never disturbed, the Appeals Court's decision leaves the project without a zoning path forward in its current form. CRG is the buyer under a pending purchase and sale agreement for roughly seventy-two acres of land from New Hopping Brook Realty Trust, sited in Holliston's industrial zoning district. In 2019, CRG applied to the planning board for site plan approval to build the warehouse and distribution facility, a project that would include 423 trailer truck spaces, 170 loading docks and 129 passenger vehicle parking spaces. The planning board approved the site plan in March 2020 with thirty-one conditions, though the town's building inspector flagged a concern at the time that the use might ultimately require a special permit for general industrial uses rather than qualifying under the bylaw's warehouse category. That concern proved prescient. In June 2020, CRG applied for a special permit while maintaining that none was actually required, and separately sought approval of a modified site plan with fewer trailer spaces and loading docks. After eleven public hearings, the planning board denied both the special permit and the modified site plan in July 2021, citing concerns about traffic, noise and the project's impact on the town's historical and agricultural character. CRG responded by suing in the Land Court on two tracks: a direct appeal of the board's denials under G. L. c. 40A, Section 17, and a separate declaratory judgment claim under G. L. c. 240, Section 14A, arguing that its warehouse was a use permitted by right under the bylaw's Section III.G.1, covering 'wholesale office or showroom, including warehouse facilities,' so that no special permit was needed in the first place. A Land Court judge agreed with CRG on the declaratory judgment count, reasoning that the bylaw's specific use of the word 'warehouse' in Section III.G.1, and nowhere else in its table of uses, meant the principal use of a property as a warehouse was allowed as of right in the industrial district. A judgment entered declaring that CRG needed no special permit and remanding the separate site-plan dispute to the planning board for further review. The town and planning board appealed, and the Appeals Court reversed. The panel agreed with CRG that no deference was owed to the board's interpretation of the use tables for purposes of the declaratory judgment claim, since that statute does not involve review of an existing board decision, unlike a direct zoning appeal. But reviewing the bylaw independently, the panel agreed with the town on the merits: given the scale of CRG's proposed facility, the project falls under the bylaw's separate category for general industrial uses exceeding 15,000 square feet of floor area, not the as-of-right warehouse category CRG had invoked, so a special permit is required after all. The practical upshot for logistics and warehouse developers is that a zoning bylaw's use table cannot be read by matching a keyword like 'warehouse' to a permitted-as-of-right category without accounting for separate, size-based use categories the same bylaw may impose on larger facilities. A roughly 800,000-square-foot distribution center with hundreds of trailer spaces and loading docks can fall outside a town's ordinary warehouse use classification even when that classification exists elsewhere in the same bylaw, pushing the project into a discretionary special-permit process that neighbors and local officials can use to raise traffic, noise and character objections. Developers assembling large industrial sites should confirm, before signing a purchase agreement, whether local bylaws tie use classification to project size or intensity, and should not assume that a favorable declaratory judgment on that question at the trial level will survive an appeal once the underlying discretionary permit denial is already final.
live-295: Florida's Fourth District Court of Appeal affirmed in part and reversed in part a trial court judgment arising from a payment dispute between two contractors on a five-story hotel project, in an opinion issued October 14, 2026. The court upheld a finding that GSD Contracting, LLC breached its subcontract with All American Builders & Debris Removal, Inc. by withholding a $71,582.98 retainage, but reversed a separate $45,300 the trial court had also awarded All American for work it never performed, since the subcontractor itself had never sought that amount. All American was the framing, drywall, insulation and acoustical-ceiling subcontractor on the hotel project. After the original general contractor was terminated, GSD Contracting took over as the replacement general contractor. The subcontract's termination-for-convenience clause allowed GSD to terminate without cause, but it entitled All American to recover payment for all subcontract work performed through the date of termination, plus demobilization costs, while expressly barring any recovery for work not yet performed, including lost profit on it. A separate retainage provision required GSD to hold back ten percent of each partial payment until ninety days after the project's final completion. By the time GSD took over the project, All American had completed roughly 93.9% of its scope and was owed a $71,582.98 retainage, with its remaining work held up because other trades had not yet finished theirs. The project then suffered significant mold issues from water intrusion. All American refused to complete its remaining work until the mold was properly remediated, citing worker safety; GSD maintained it had already done enough by removing some drywall and running limited mold testing, without hiring an industrial hygienist or preparing a formal remediation plan. GSD terminated All American from the project and never paid out the retainage. All American sued GSD for breach of contract, seeking only the $71,582.98 retainage; at trial, its owner testified that the company was not pursuing the separate $45,300 figure tied to unperformed work. The trial court nonetheless found GSD had breached the subcontract both by failing to pay the retainage and by failing to properly remediate the mold, and awarded All American $116,882.98 — the full retainage plus the $45,300 nobody had asked for. On appeal, the Fourth District held the contract's plain language supported the retainage award on its own: the ninety-day holdback period had long since expired once the project was completed in 2023, and nothing in the subcontract let GSD withhold the retainage based on an alleged default once there was no termination-for-cause clause to invoke. Because that ground was sufficient to affirm, the court did not need to reach whether GSD had also breached by failing to remediate the mold. It reversed the $45,300 award outright, since All American had conceded it was never sought and the subcontract's own termination-for-convenience language barred recovery for work not performed. The ruling is a useful case study for general contractors managing distressed construction projects, particularly one taken over mid-stream. A retainage clause tied to a fixed post-completion holdback period functions as a near-automatic payment obligation once that period runs, and a contractor cannot convert a safety or remediation dispute into an offset against retainage unless the subcontract itself gives it that right through a termination-for-cause or similar provision. Courts will also hold a plaintiff to the damages it actually pleaded and proved at trial, so a trial court cannot award more than what was sought merely because it also found an independent breach. Contractors on both sides of these disputes should review what their subcontracts actually say about for-cause termination, offsets and retainage timing before relying on a default theory to withhold payment, and should keep clear documentation, such as hygienist reports and formal remediation plans, to support any remediation-based defense.
live-296: Investors have filed a federal securities fraud class action against Millrose Properties, Inc., the Miami-based land-banking REIT spun off from homebuilder Lennar Corporation in February 2025, alleging that the company and two of its top executives misrepresented its business model by secretly acquiring and renting out completed single-family homes after telling the market it would hold undeveloped land and nothing more. The case, Rubenstein et al. v. Millrose Properties, Inc. et al., No. 9:26-cv-81386, was filed October 9, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida on behalf of investors who purchased Millrose stock between February 7, 2025 and October 2, 2026. live-303: The Supreme Court of Alabama granted a writ of mandamus on October 16, 2026, directing a Baldwin County circuit court to enter judgment for the City of Fairhope and its Planning Commission on a developer's negligence claim over the denial of two apartment-complex applications, holding that both the volunteer members of the Commission and the city employees who advised them are immune from suit under Alabama law.
