live-306: A federal magistrate judge in the Southern District of Texas did not mince words at a recent hearing over a 228-unit apartment complex outside Houston: the conduct he was being asked to evaluate, he said from the bench, was "pretty damn egregious." The remark, from U.S. Magistrate Judge Andrew M. Edison of the court's Galveston Division, came in a dispute between Freddie Mac and a subsidiary of New York-based multifamily buyer Nord Group over Edgewater Apartments, a 228-unit garden-style community in Lake Jackson, Texas that Nord acquired in 2022. According to reporting on the case, Freddie Mac had already foreclosed on the property after the Nord subsidiary stopped making mortgage payments roughly eighteen months earlier, yet the former owner kept collecting rent from tenants after losing title, and then sued its own lender over the dispute rather than relinquish the proceeds. The Edgewater hearing is only the most visible flashpoint in what trade press now describes as a broader unraveling of Nord Group's multifamily portfolio. Lenders and investors across several of the company's holdings have accused Nord-affiliated entities of pocketing rents that should have gone to loan servicers, supplying fabricated insurance records to lenders and regulators, and allowing properties to fall into what one report called an "alarming state of neglect." Court filings in the broader litigation reportedly document sewage backups, mold, vermin, and other conditions rendering units uninhabitable, the kind of property-level deterioration that typically surfaces only after a landlord has stopped reinvesting operating income back into a building. Nord Group, led by its 27-year-old co-founder Saqif Noor, was among the multifamily buyers that acquired aggressively during the 2021-2022 run-up in apartment values, often using floating-rate, value-add debt that became difficult to service once interest rates rose and refinancing options narrowed. The company's financial distress has already produced a tangled bankruptcy history. Nord Group has reportedly attempted Chapter 11 protection for another of its Houston-area assets, Huntington Glen Apartments, in at least three separate venues, with a Delaware bankruptcy court marking the most recent stop after Fannie Mae sought to consolidate the company's cases in Texas. Other Nord-owned properties, including a Houston asset financed with a CMBS loan that went to special servicing, and an Austin complex headed toward a foreclosure auction, point to a pattern of a buyer that expanded quickly on leverage and has struggled on multiple fronts simultaneously as that leverage came due. What makes the Edgewater dispute legally significant is not simply that a borrower defaulted, which alone is unremarkable in today's multifamily financing environment. It is that the borrower allegedly continued to exercise de facto control over a foreclosed asset's cash flow after title had already passed to the lender, and then used litigation offensively, suing the lender rather than accounting for the rents collected. That fact pattern raises exposure well beyond an ordinary foreclosure: diverting rents from collateral a lender already owns can support claims for conversion and unjust enrichment in addition to breach of the loan documents, and a court's characterization of that conduct as egregious is the kind of judicial signal that tends to foreclose sympathetic treatment on any later equitable defenses the borrower might raise. The allegations of falsified insurance records carry their own distinct risk. Lenders routinely rely on a borrower's certified proof of insurance to protect their collateral position, and loan documents typically treat a material misrepresentation about coverage as an independent event of default, one that can, depending on the loan's recourse carve-outs, convert what would otherwise be a non-recourse workout into personal liability for the sponsors who signed the guaranty. Special servicers and lenders increasingly scrutinize insurance certificates as an early-warning signal precisely because fabricating them is both easy to allege and difficult for a distressed borrower to explain away. For lenders and special servicers managing a multifamily book that includes 2021-2022 vintage acquisitions, the Nord Group situation is a reminder to move quickly once a maturity default is identified, both to secure possession and rent streams through a receiver and to audit a defaulting borrower's insurance certifications and reported property conditions rather than relying on self-reported compliance. For sponsors facing their own liquidity strain, the case illustrates that litigating against a lender after a foreclosure has already been entered is a high-risk strategy: a court that views continued rent collection as self-help rather than a good-faith dispute is unlikely to extend much benefit of the doubt on the underlying merits, and a judicial finding of bad-faith conduct can reopen avenues to personal liability that a purely financial default would not.
live-307: A creative office campus built on the bones of a shuttered Macy's department store in West Los Angeles has landed in default, with its lender, ACORE Capital, declaring that developer GPI Companies owes more than $80 million on the project. Public records reviewed by The Real Deal and WestsideToday show ACORE recorded a notice of default against GPI in September 2026 after the developer failed to make required payments on the debt secured by West End, a 235,000-square-foot office campus at 10730 West Pico Boulevard. The notice marks a sharp reversal for a project that, on paper, should have benefited from one of the Westside's more creative adaptive-reuse stories. GPI purchased the shuttered Macy's store and an adjoining parking structure at the former Westside Pavilion mall in an off-market deal in 2017, then converted the site into creative office space aimed at entertainment, media, and technology tenants. Construction financing came from ACORE Capital, reported at $120 million in 2019; the parties are separately reported to have entered a $97.6 million refinancing agreement in 2024 once the building was substantially complete. The two outlets' accounts differ on exactly how that 2024 debt relates to the original construction note, but both agree the campus, completed in 2022, has apparently never signed an anchor tenant and appears to sit entirely vacant today, based on marketing materials and site observations cited in the reporting. For a project whose marketing has long centered on move-in-ready creative space, zero recorded leasing activity four years after completion is itself a significant data point, independent of the default. Neither GPI's co-founders and managing partners, Cliff Goldstein and Drew Planting, nor representatives for ACORE Capital responded to requests for comment reported in the coverage, leaving the borrower's plan for curing the default, if any, unclear. California is a non-judicial foreclosure state, meaning ACORE does not need to file a lawsuit to foreclose; recording a notice of default under California Civil Code Section 2924 is itself the formal first step in the trustee's-sale process that can culminate in a public auction of the property, typically several months after the notice is recorded, absent a cure, forbearance agreement, or negotiated workout. GPI's position here is a familiar one in the current cycle for sponsors who financed speculative office conversions during the low-rate years preceding 2022: the underlying real estate thesis ran into a leasing market that has been unusually slow to absorb new office product built on spec without a signed anchor, leaving the borrower with little operating income to service the debt and correspondingly little leverage in workout negotiations. For commercial real estate sponsors with vacant or under-leased spec office product nearing a loan maturity or refinancing deadline, the West End default is a reminder that a strong physical asset and a sound redevelopment concept do not, by themselves, generate the operating cash flow a lender needs to see before extending further patience. Borrowers facing a similar gap between completion and lease-up should engage lenders proactively, well before a scheduled payment is missed, documenting a credible leasing pipeline, since post-default negotiating leverage in a non-judicial foreclosure state weakens quickly once the statutory trustee's-sale clock starts running; lenders and special servicers evaluating workouts on comparable vacant creative-office collateral should treat this default as a cautionary data point on the risk of financing speculative office product without a leasing covenant or pre-leasing threshold built into the loan documents.
live-308: A three-building office campus in North San Jose that serves as the corporate headquarters of air-taxi developer Archer Aviation has fallen into default after its owner failed to repay an $80 million loan at maturity, according to reporting by The Real Deal and The Registry. The campus, located at 190, 210, and 230 West Tasman Drive and totaling roughly 287,370 square feet, is owned by an affiliate of KU Education, which was served with a notice of default in October after the loan, originated by Jefferies LoanCore in 2016, matured unpaid in August 2026. Archer Aviation's headquarters occupies the 190 West Tasman building, and the company also leases the adjoining 210 West Tasman building; the campus's 230 West Tasman building was previously leased to smart-meter maker Itron before that company relocated its own headquarters to nearby Santa Clara. Archer's presence as the anchor tenant means the dispute between KU Education and its lender sits directly beneath one of Silicon Valley's more closely watched growth companies, even though Archer itself is not a party to the loan default and its lease obligations are unaffected by the ownership-level dispute. The default follows a now-familiar arc for commercial mortgages originated in the mid-2010s on long amortization schedules: a loan that priced and underwrote comfortably a decade ago matures into a dramatically higher interest-rate environment, and a refinancing that once would have been routine instead requires fresh equity, a rate the borrower cannot support, or a lender unwilling to extend on the existing terms. Jefferies LoanCore's decision to proceed to a notice of default, rather than negotiate an extension, suggests the entity managing the loan concluded that further forbearance was not in its interest, a judgment that often turns on updated appraisals showing the collateral's value relative to the outstanding debt. As in other California commercial foreclosures, the notice of default recorded against the KU Education affiliate is not a lawsuit; it is the formal trigger for the state's non-judicial trustee's-sale process under California Civil Code Section 2924, which, absent a cure or negotiated resolution, proceeds toward a public trustee's sale on a statutory timeline measured in months. The reported default sits in a broader pattern of North San Jose office distress this month: a separate four-building campus a few miles away that once housed eBay's offices has also fallen into default, with Deutsche Bank the lender there, suggesting that mid-2010s-vintage office debt across the submarket is coming due into a market that has not fully recovered its pre-pandemic occupancy or valuations. Owners of commercial office assets financed on 2015-2018-vintage mortgages approaching maturity should assume lenders are underwriting refinancing requests against current, not origination-era, valuations and interest rates, and should begin workout conversations well before a scheduled maturity date rather than after a missed payment, since the leverage shift once a notice of default is recorded can be significant and fast-moving in a non-judicial state. Tenants in buildings facing an ownership-level loan default, including anchor tenants like Archer Aviation here, should confirm that a change in ownership through foreclosure would not itself constitute a default or termination right under their own lease, since a foreclosing lender typically takes title subject to existing leases but tenants are often unaware of their own protections until a dispute arises.
live-309: A four-building North San Jose office campus once occupied by eBay is sliding toward a full foreclosure after its owners defaulted on an $88.1 million loan, with the unpaid balance now reported at $98.4 million as accrued interest, fees, and default charges continue to mount. The Real Deal and Hoodline report that Deutsche Bank AG, the lender, filed an initial notice of default against the campus's owners, Ocean West Capital Partners and Hana Asset Management, in July 2026, and that sources familiar with the matter say Deutsche Bank now plans to proceed with a complete foreclosure rather than negotiate a further extension. The 250,100-square-foot campus, located at 2515, 2525, 2535, and 2545 North First Street, was acquired by the Ocean West and Hana partnership for $132.5 million in 2018, a period when Silicon Valley office product commanded some of the highest valuations in the country. eBay had occupied the campus as part of its broader San Jose footprint but vacated in 2020 to consolidate operations at its main headquarters in the city's Willow Glen district; under the terms of its lease, eBay continued paying rent on the vacated space for several years before that obligation terminated in March 2026, removing what had been the ownership group's primary income stream just as the loan's troubles were becoming acute. Citing Morningstar Credit data relayed by the Bay Area News Group, the reports put the campus's current value at approximately $54.7 million, a decline of roughly 59% from the $132.5 million purchase price seven years ago. That gap between the shrinking collateral value and the growing unpaid loan balance, now nearly double the property's estimated worth, illustrates why Deutsche Bank's reported decision to pursue a full foreclosure, rather than continue extending or restructuring the debt, tracks a now-common lender calculus: once an appraisal shows the loan meaningfully underwater and the asset generates no offsetting rental income, a consensual workout offers the lender little advantage over simply taking title and remarketing the property. Notably, The Real Deal's coverage indicates that prospective buyers, including Goodman Group and Harvest Properties, are already circling the campus in anticipation of a foreclosure sale or a negotiated transfer, even before the trustee's-sale process has concluded. That early interest reflects a broader dynamic in the current cycle: well-capitalized buyers are increasingly willing to underwrite vacant, distressed office assets at a sufficient discount to replacement cost in supply-constrained Silicon Valley submarkets, betting that today's trough valuations will prove a durable long-term basis even if near-term leasing remains slow. As with other California commercial mortgage defaults, Deutsche Bank's notice of default is a non-judicial filing under California Civil Code Section 2924 rather than a court complaint, proceeding toward a public trustee's sale on a statutory timeline unless the parties reach a deed-in-lieu or other negotiated transfer first. Owners of vacant or soon-to-be-vacant single-tenant office assets should treat a departing anchor tenant's final rent payment date as a hard deadline for either securing replacement income or finalizing a workout with the lender, since a lender's patience during a tenant's wind-down period often evaporates once that income stream actually stops. Lenders and special servicers holding debt on comparable vacant Silicon Valley office campuses should expect this foreclosure, if completed, to become a closely watched comparable sale given the scale of the value decline already reflected in third-party appraisals, and prospective buyers circling distressed assets ahead of a completed foreclosure should confirm through counsel exactly what interest they would be acquiring, since a loan purchase, a post-foreclosure REO purchase, and a negotiated deed-in-lieu each carry different title, environmental, and holdover-tenant risk.
live-310: A Texas Court of Appeals panel has affirmed summary judgment for a Harwin-area Houston shopping center ownership group, rejecting a restaurant tenant's claims for breach of lease, fraud, violations of the Deceptive Trade Practices Act, and quantum meruit arising from a long-running dispute over repair costs and a refused sublease. The October 16, 2026 memorandum opinion traces back to an October 2019 lease, written on a standard Texas Association of Realtors form, for a restaurant space on Richmond Avenue in Houston, which divided maintenance responsibilities between landlord and tenant in ways that proved decisive on appeal. Under the lease, the landlord bore responsibility only for roof repairs, and only after the tenant gave written notice of the need for one; the tenant was responsible for grounds, parking, plumbing, drainage and the HVAC system, including a mandatory maintenance contract. The tenant alleged that after the landlord's interest was assigned to a successor ownership entity in January 2021, without proper notice, it spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on repairs and improvements the landlord refused to reimburse, and that the landlord's principal had separately promised to consent to a sublease and sale of the restaurant business. Relying on that promise, the tenant located a buyer and executed an estoppel certificate, attesting the landlord was not in default, as a condition of pursuing the deal -- only for the landlord to refuse consent to the sublease after the fact. A materialmen's lien followed once the tenant told its vendors the landlord would not cover the improvement costs. The trial court granted the landlord's hybrid summary judgment motion on every claim, and the Court of Appeals affirmed each ground. The breach-of-lease claims failed because the lease itself assigned electrical, plumbing and HVAC maintenance to the tenant, and because the tenant offered no evidence it ever gave the landlord the written notice the lease required before claiming a roof-repair default; the lease's as-is acceptance clause and disclaimer of warranties independently defeated any claim that the landlord had to repair the roof before move-in. The oral sublease-consent promise failed under the statute of frauds, since the proposed sublease term exceeded one year and Texas law requires such agreements to be in writing. The DTPA holding is the opinion's most broadly instructive point. Texas law exempts from DTPA coverage any transaction tied to a single nonresidential project where the consumer's total consideration exceeds $500,000. The lease's sixty-month term at $8,700 in monthly base rent totaled $522,000 -- just over that threshold -- which the trial court cited as an independent, unrebutted basis to dismiss the DTPA claim. The fraud claim was likewise dismissed on a procedural ground: the tenant failed to replead it after the trial court sustained special exceptions, leaving nothing live for the court to review. For commercial landlords and tenants, the decision is a reminder that maintenance-allocation clauses and notice preconditions are enforced on their literal terms, and that a tenant cannot convert a landlord's general awareness of a problem into a breach claim without satisfying whatever written-notice mechanism the lease specifies. The case is also a caution about estoppel certificates signed to grease a pending transaction: the tenant's own representation that the landlord was not in default became one more obstacle once the relationship soured. And for parties structuring longer commercial leases, the DTPA's $500,000 nonresidential-transaction exemption is worth calculating early, since crossing that line -- as this sixty-month, $8,700-a-month lease did by a comparatively modest margin -- removes a tenant's consumer-protection remedy entirely, independent of how the lease's own terms are ultimately construed.
live-311: The Appellate Division, First Department has affirmed the dismissal of a SoHo landlord's claims against the individual guarantors of a retail lease, holding that their personal liability ended when the tenant physically vacated the premises -- regardless of a separate lease provision that purported to extend liability until a later, formally defined 'Surrender Date.' The October 1, 2026 decision in 62 Wooster, LLC v. TML N.Y. Inc. is among the first significant applications of the New York Court of Appeals' 2025 ruling in 1995 CAM LLC v. West Side Advisors, and it gives landlords and counsel a clearer picture of how good guy guaranty release language will be read when a lease's own provisions conflict. The case concerns a retail lease at 476 Broome Street in Manhattan. Two individuals each executed substantively identical personal good guy guaranties in connection with the tenant's lease -- a standard device in New York City commercial leasing that typically limits a principal's personal exposure to the period before the tenant vacates, in exchange for the tenant leaving the space broom clean and giving timely notice. The guaranty documents here contained two provisions in tension: a surrender clause ending liability for rent accruing after the tenant 'surrendered legal possession,' a phrase the guaranties never defined, and a separate good guy provision purporting to keep the guarantors liable through a defined 'Surrender Date' tied to the broader lease documents rather than the simple fact of vacatur. According to the record, the tenant vacated by tendering keys to the landlord's agent and delivering the premises broom clean in the fall of 2020. The landlord nonetheless sued the individual guarantors, seeking approximately $307,577.08 in unpaid rent for July through October 2021, liquidated damages measured by the shortfall between the lease rent and what the landlord collected upon reletting through the original lease's expiration date, and its costs of enforcing the guaranty. Supreme Court, New York County (Alexander M. Tisch, J.), granted the guarantors' motion to dismiss those claims, and the landlord appealed. The First Department affirmed, without costs, applying 1995 CAM LLC's construction of 'surrender' in a commercial guaranty to mean the tenant's physical relinquishment of possession and control -- not the landlord's subsequent acceptance, and not a later-defined contractual milestone layered on top of the physical fact of vacatur. Applying that rule, the panel held the guarantors' liability ended when the tenant relinquished possession in 2020, notwithstanding the landlord's argument that the lease documents' own 'Surrender Date' concept had never been triggered. The practical effect was to foreclose the landlord's unpaid-rent, liquidated-damages and enforcement-cost claims against the guarantors in full, even though the landlord's theory found some textual support in the guaranty's own 'Surrender Date' language. For landlords, the lesson is to reconcile any provision intended to extend guarantor liability beyond actual vacatur with the guaranty's own surrender or release clause at the drafting stage, rather than leaving the two to conflict. Tenants and guarantors, meanwhile, should carefully document the date and manner of vacatur -- delivery of keys, broom-clean condition, and written notice to the landlord's agent -- since that evidentiary record is now squarely what determines when liability ends under this line of cases, and landlords seeking rent, reletting shortfalls or enforcement costs from a guarantor after a tenant has left should expect courts to read any ambiguity against the drafter.
live-312: Shadowbox Studios, the Atlanta-area production company behind films including Cocaine Bear, has sued DeKalb County, Georgia, alleging that a moratorium on new data center development unlawfully blocks a project the county had already told the company it could build. The lawsuit, filed August 5, 2026 by Shadowbox and an affiliated entity, Henrico 183, in DeKalb County Superior Court, asks a judge to declare the moratorium invalid as applied to the company's roughly 200-acre property at 3600 International Park Drive, to clear the way for construction, and to award just compensation for what the complaint characterizes as a violation of the company's property rights, along with attorneys' fees. According to the complaint, Shadowbox and Henrico 183 have spent more than $30 million developing the International Park Drive site for data center use, acting in reliance on representations from DeKalb County planning staff that a data center was an allowed use on the property. The county has pushed back on that characterization, with planning officials stating that any letters sent to the company were never intended to function as legally binding commitments. DeKalb enacted its first temporary moratorium on new data center applications in July 2025 and has extended it multiple times since, with reporting indicating the freeze now runs through March 2027 while the county drafts permanent rules addressing the power, water, and infrastructure demands of large-scale data center campuses. The financial stakes described in public reporting vary depending on the source and the stage of the dispute: Shadowbox has cited figures ranging from roughly $30 million to more than $37 million invested or at risk in different filings, and the company's chief executive, Peter Rumbold, has been quoted putting the company's total exposure above $100 million. The lawsuit itself alleges the moratorium has cut the property's value by as much as $200 million. Those figures have not been tested in court and reflect one side's characterization pending further proceedings. The litigation has not stayed confined to the courthouse. On September 9, 2026, DeKalb County's Zoning Board of Appeals voted to affirm its earlier denial of Shadowbox's data center proposal, with board members citing the pending lawsuit as a reason for leaving the underlying zoning question to the courts. Counsel for Shadowbox argued before the board that the county never provided proper public notice or an opportunity to be heard when it originally passed, and later extended, the moratorium, a procedural objection that, if it gains traction, could complicate the county's defense of the moratorium independent of the takings question. Data center moratoria have become one of the fastest-growing sources of land-use litigation in the country over the past two years, as local governments confronted with power-hungry, politically contentious projects reach for temporary freezes while they study infrastructure impacts and draft more durable zoning frameworks. Developers on the losing end of those freezes are increasingly pairing the traditional vested-rights argument, that an application submitted before a moratorium took effect should be judged under the old rules, with regulatory-takings claims seeking money damages for the diminution in value a prolonged freeze causes. The Shadowbox case shows why that pairing has obvious appeal: if a county's own planning staff can be shown to have represented, even informally, that a use was permitted, a subsequent moratorium blocking that specific, already-represented project looks far more like a targeted taking than a neutral, generally applicable pause. For developers evaluating a large-scale commercial project in a jurisdiction considering or already enforcing a moratorium, the practical lesson is to get any planning-staff representation about permitted use in writing, confirm whether the jurisdiction treats that writing as binding, and build a paper trail documenting reliance and expenditures from the date of that representation forward, since both will matter once a moratorium intervenes; to treat a moratorium as more than a timing problem and, with counsel, weigh whether the facts support a regulatory-takings theory rather than relying on vested-rights arguments alone, particularly where the freeze appears to target a specific project rather than a land-use category generally; and to scrutinize the moratorium ordinance's own procedural history, including whether required public notice and hearing procedures were followed and whether it has been extended beyond its original term, since defects in the moratorium's adoption can provide an independent line of attack alongside the takings claim itself.
live-313: Developers who clear a rezoning and a variance through a city council often treat that approval as the end of the entitlement fight. A decision issued October 19, 2026 by the Supreme Court of Ohio is a reminder that in a chartered municipality with initiative and referendum rights, the city council's vote can be only the opening round. In State ex rel. Sommers Development Group, L.L.C. v. Cuyahoga County Board of Elections, the court unanimously denied a developer's request for writs of prohibition and mandamus that would have kept a citizen-driven referendum off the November 3, 2026 ballot, clearing the way for voters in Mayfield Heights to decide whether to reverse a zoning change the city council had already approved for a planned townhome community. Sommers Development Group, LLC is the developer under contract with Rockwell Automation, Inc., which owns the property, to redevelop a parcel in Mayfield Heights, a Cleveland suburb, from an office-park use into a townhome community. To do so, Sommers needed the city to rezone the land from a Headquarters or Executive Offices Park District classification to a Planned Unit Development District classification, along with a density variance and preliminary site-plan approval. On May 27, 2026, the Mayfield Heights City Council granted all of it, adopting the rezoning ordinance and a resolution approving the variance. That might have ended the matter, but Ohio municipal charters commonly reserve initiative and referendum powers to the electorate, and Mayfield Heights' charter is no exception. On July 24, 2026, a citizens' committee opposed to the project submitted a petition seeking an ordinance that would return the property to its prior zoning classification. After a hearing that produced no vote, the city council held a special meeting on September 1 and voted 4-3 not to adopt the committee's proposed ordinance itself, which, under the charter's initiative mechanism, sends the question to the voters rather than ending it. The committee then filed a supplemental petition to shore up its signature count, and the Cuyahoga County Board of Elections determined the petition carried 691 valid signatures, more than enough to qualify. On September 9, the council authorized certification of the initiative to the ballot for the November 3 general election. Sommers protested to the board of elections the next day, arguing the petition was procedurally defective on four grounds: that it was really an untimely referendum petition dressed up as an initiative; that the underlying zoning action was an administrative act not subject to referendum at all; that the petition committee and council had not complied with the charter's own requirements for placing an initiative on the ballot; and that the council had certified the petition to the board after the statutory deadline. The board held a hearing on September 21 and denied the protest. Sommers took its case directly to the Ohio Supreme Court four days later, seeking an emergency order either barring the board from placing the measure on the ballot or directing it to grant the protest. The board of elections and the intervening petition committee first argued Sommers had waited too long, invoking the doctrine of laches. The court rejected that defense outright, holding that Sommers acted within a day of the council's certification resolution in filing its protest, and within four days of the protest's denial in filing suit, timelines the board and committee did not themselves characterize as unreasonable. Having cleared that procedural hurdle, Sommers still lost: the court held Sommers failed to show the board of elections abused its discretion or clearly disregarded applicable law when it certified the initiative and rejected Sommers' protest, and denied both writs. The referendum stays on the November 3 ballot, and Mayfield Heights voters, not the courts, will decide whether the rezoning that cleared the way for Sommers' townhome project survives. For commercial developers, the case is a pointed illustration of a risk that is easy to underweight during entitlement planning in charter municipalities with initiative and referendum rights: a council approval is not necessarily the final word, and courts will extend real procedural latitude to election boards processing a citizen challenge to that approval, even while giving a developer the benefit of the doubt on how quickly it had to object. Winning the laches argument did Sommers no good once the merits went against it, and developers facing a possible referendum fight should budget for the political and ballot-box risk separately from the zoning-approval process itself, scrutinize a municipality's charter provisions on initiative, referendum and certification deadlines before relying on a council vote as final, and recognize that Ohio courts have shown little appetite to second-guess a board of elections' procedural calls absent a clear abuse of discretion or a clear disregard of the law.
live-314: A California appeals court has affirmed a trial court judgment confirming an arbitration award in favor of a Los Angeles landlord in a years-long commercial lease dispute that began with a disagreement over a 3,000-gallon grease interceptor and ended in a fraud trial, a jury mistrial, and binding arbitration. The case, The Waffle, LLC v. Tucker Investment Group, LLC, decided October 19, 2026 by the California Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District, Division Seven, shows how far courts will defer to arbitrators once commercial parties agree to arbitrate a lease dispute. The dispute traces to a March 30, 2017 lease between Tucker Investment Group, LLC (TIG), the master lessee of a commercial property in Westwood, and The Waffle, LLC, which planned to open a second restaurant location there. Under a construction work letter attached to the lease, TIG agreed to install a four-inch grease waste line connected to a 3,000-gallon grease interceptor, but the parties never fixed a firm deadline for the work. Instead the lease relied on a cure provision requiring TIG to act within a 'reasonable time' after written notice of default -- no less than 30 days, or, if the obligation could not reasonably be finished within 30 days, commencement within that window followed by diligent pursuit to completion. That ambiguity became the center of the fight. From late 2017 into early 2018, TIG's project manager and The Waffle's principal went back and forth over whether a smaller 'Schier' grease trap could substitute for the bulkier interceptor, which required costly excavation behind the premises. When The Waffle's side rejected the substitute as final in April 2018, it sent TIG a formal notice of breach; TIG responded that it was returning to engineers to plan installation of the original unit. The Waffle sued on May 2, 2018, alleging fraud and negligent misrepresentation against TIG and its project manager's firm, Coastline Construction Management, Inc., and seeking rescission and breach-of-contract relief against TIG. The case proceeded in two phases. In a 2021 bench trial on the breach-of-contract claim, the trial court sided with TIG, reasoning that under the lease's cure language a landlord is not in breach merely for missing an ambitious timeline, only for failing to commence a non-30-day obligation within 30 days and thereafter diligently pursue it; because TIG had engaged engineers and moved toward installing the original interceptor, the court found no breach. A 2022 jury trial on the fraud claims produced a mistrial after a deadlock, and rather than retry those claims, the parties stipulated to binding arbitration under ADR Services, Inc. rules, waiving any right to appeal except on narrow statutory grounds. The arbitrator ruled for TIG, and the trial court confirmed the award over The Waffle's objections that the arbitrator exceeded his authority, failed to issue a reasoned award, and wrongly awarded fees tied to settled co-defendants. The Court of Appeal rejected each of The Waffle's arguments and affirmed in full, underscoring that once parties stipulate to binding arbitration with an appellate-rights waiver, California courts will not relitigate the merits on review -- an arbitrator's reliance on prior findings from the same litigation, a terse award, and a fee award touching settled co-defendants all fall well within the narrow discretion appellate courts give arbitrators under the state's arbitration statute. The ruling is also a reminder that a lease's own cure-period language can do more work than any later factual dispute: here, the operative question was never really whether TIG delayed, but whether the lease's 30-day commence-and-diligently-pursue standard was satisfied, and that framework effectively decided the contract claim long before arbitration ever began. For commercial landlords and tenants negotiating construction work letters or tenant-improvement obligations, the case offers a few practical lessons: build a specific, unambiguous deadline into any obligation tied to major capital work like a grease interceptor rather than relying on open-ended 'reasonable time' cure language that can be litigated for years; recognize that agreeing to binding arbitration, especially with an appellate-rights waiver, effectively forecloses a second look at the merits, so that decision should be made with full awareness of the stakes; and understand that a prevailing party's fee award in arbitration can extend to work connected to co-defendants who settled earlier in the case, so fee exposure should be sized against the full scope of the litigation rather than just the arbitrating parties.
live-315: A foreclosure sale that had been scheduled for October 29, 2026 at the Hall of Justice in Rochester, New York is on hold after the owner of the Hungerford Building -- a roughly 3.4-acre, century-old mixed-use complex on East Main Street long known as an artist-studio hub -- filed an appeal challenging the referee's report underlying the foreclosure judgment. The appeal, reported by the Rochester Business Journal and the Daily Record on October 15, 2026, pauses what had looked like the final step in a foreclosure case that has run for more than a year. The case was brought by lender Elizon DB Transfer Agent LLC against The Hungerford Building LLC, HB Factory LLC and PH Realty Capital LLC, the entities that control the former soda-syrup factory complex at 1115 East Main Street. The borrower entities acquired the building in 2022 with an $8.25 million loan; after an earlier default, the parties signed a forbearance agreement extending the loan's maturity to December 2024. Payments again lapsed, and Elizon pursued foreclosure in Monroe County Supreme Court before Justice Daniel J. Doyle. Doyle granted summary judgment of foreclosure earlier in 2026, and the case proceeded to a court-appointed referee to compute the amount due. The referee's report put the figure at $10,490,036.37, substantially above the original loan balance once accrued interest, fees and forbearance-period costs were layered on. In September 2026, Doyle confirmed the referee's report and authorized a sale, which the referee calendared for October 29. That is where the case stood until early October, when an attorney for the Hungerford-affiliated defendants filed a notice of appeal, arguing that Doyle's order relied on a flawed referee's report and that summary judgment should not have been granted on the record as it stood. The appeal automatically paused the scheduled auction. The building's owner has told local reporters he intends to pay off the roughly $10.4 million balance before any bids are taken, which could moot the sale regardless of how the appeal is resolved. The dispute is a compact illustration of several recurring commercial-foreclosure dynamics for owners and lenders alike. For lenders and special servicers, the lesson is about timing as much as substance: once a referee's report is confirmed and a sale date is set, it is tempting to treat the auction as all but final, but a represented borrower can still interrupt that process at the eleventh hour. Workout teams should keep payoff and settlement channels open through the appellate window, scrutinize the strength of the underlying referee computation before relying on a scheduled sale date, and recognize that buildings carrying legacy, below-market tenancies -- like the Hungerford's long-time artist studios -- can add both reputational pressure and negotiating leverage to a contested foreclosure on both sides of the table.
live-316: The Ohio Supreme Court on October 20, 2026 denied a writ of mandamus sought by a data-center developer against the Village of Lordstown, holding that a temporary moratorium on new data-center permits left the village with no clear legal duty to process the developer's site plan under the zoning rules in effect when the application was submitted. For developers, the practical lesson is to treat zoning risk as live all the way through permit issuance rather than just through application filing, since mandamus and vested-rights doctrines generally protect a completed review process far more reliably than a pending one; to front-load community engagement before filing rather than relying on the formal site-plan timeline to outpace local opposition; and, where a municipality has already signaled opposition to a use through a committee recommendation or pending council vote, to plan deal timelines and land-acquisition contingencies around the real possibility of a parallel legislative response, including a moratorium enacted mid-litigation.
live-317: New York's Appellate Division, First Department ruled on October 20, 2026 that New York City's so-called "guaranty law" -- which barred landlords from enforcing personal guaranties on certain commercial leases for a 16-month window during the COVID-19 pandemic -- does not violate the Contracts Clause of the U.S. Constitution. The decision, in 513 West 26th Realty LLC v. George Billis Galleries, Inc., reverses a trial court ruling that had struck the law down, and it lands in the middle of a yearslong, unsettled fight between state and federal courts over the measure's constitutionality. The case arose from an ordinary pandemic-era rent dispute. Landlord 513 West 26th Realty LLC leased Chelsea space to George Billis Galleries, Inc., an art exhibition business, with gallery principal George Billis personally guarantying the tenant's lease obligations. When the gallery stopped paying rent during the pandemic, the landlord sued the tenant for breach of the lease and the guarantor for breach of the guaranty. On remand, Supreme Court this time declared the guaranty law unconstitutional under the Contracts Clause, reinstated the landlord's claims against the guarantor, and denied motions to dismiss filed by both the tenant and the City of New York, which had intervened to defend its own ordinance. A substantial population of pre-2020 personal guaranties tied to commercial leases remain the subject of active collection litigation in New York courts, and landlords and guarantors alike have been litigating in the shadow of conflicting signals -- first a federal district court finding the law unconstitutional, then a federal appellate vacatur that left the question unresolved, and now a state appellate ruling going the other way. The First Department's decision does not bind federal courts, and the Second Circuit has not yet ruled on the law's merits following the Bochner vacatur, so the conflict is not fully resolved, but it is now the controlling word for guaranty disputes litigated in New York's state courts, where the great majority of these cases are filed. Landlords pressing or considering guaranty claims tied to 2020 and 2021 defaults should factor this ruling into settlement posture rather than assume federal precedent will rescue a guaranty claim in state court, while guarantors facing collection suits on legacy pandemic defaults gain a reaffirmed shield in the First Department, at least until further appellate activity -- whether by the City seeking to cement the win elsewhere or by guarantors testing the ruling's reach in other departments -- resolves the conflict more fully.
live-318: Two West Palm Beach neighborhood associations sued Palm Beach County, the City of West Palm Beach, its Community Redevelopment Agency, the CityPlace Community Development District, and affiliates of developer Related Ross on October 14, 2026, seeking to void the county's approval of a $26 million public financing package for a planned 400-room convention center hotel. The complaint, filed in Florida's Fifteenth Judicial Circuit by the Grandview Heights Neighborhood Association and the West Palm Beach Neighborhood Alliance, does not challenge the hotel's design or its zoning entitlements directly. A commission's compliance with a bare statutory minimum does not necessarily immunize a vote from a reasonable-notice challenge when the underlying documentation is unusually voluminous or was supplied at the last minute. For developers structuring complex sale-leaseback or incentive packages with local governments, the direction of this case will matter well beyond West Palm Beach: large, multi-part transactions that surface for a vote only shortly before the meeting are an increasingly visible target for neighborhood litigants looking to unwind a deal after the fact, and a void-ab-initio finding can put months of pre-construction work and committed public financing back into limbo. Developers and public-sector partners negotiating similar deals should push for complete transaction packages to be posted well ahead of a scheduled vote, build a contemporaneous record of when materials actually became available, and expect that once substantive zoning fights are resolved or losing traction, organized opposition will increasingly look to process-based openings like this one.
live-319: New York's Appellate Division, Second Department ruled on October 21, 2026 that a Brooklyn commercial sublessor was not entitled to summary judgment on a $1,004,426.20 unpaid-rent judgment, because its sublessee raised a genuine factual dispute over whether the sublessor itself had breached the sublease. The decision, VK Dental Group, Inc. v. Tender Touch Physical Therapy, PLLC, reverses a Supreme Court, Kings County judgment and sends the underlying rent dispute back for further proceedings. The case traces back to a chain of leasing transactions involving commercial office space. In January 2017, Metrotech Smile Dental, P.C. leased the property from nonparty landlord 350 Fulton Realty, LLC. Two months later, Metrotech subleased the premises to Tender Touch Physical Therapy, PLLC and other sublessees. In April 2018, Metrotech assigned its prime lease to VK Dental Group, Inc., which took over as sublessor to the Tender Touch defendants. On appeal, the Second Department applied New York's four-part test for a breach-of-contract claim: the existence of a contract, the plaintiff's own performance, the defendant's breach, and resulting damages. The panel agreed VK Dental met its initial burden by showing the sublessees had not paid rent for certain months, but held that the sublessees defeated summary judgment by submitting the affidavit of their principal, who testified that VK Dental itself failed to pay 50% of the premises' utility costs as the sublease required, and had the gas service to the premises disconnected. Because a breach-of-contract plaintiff must also establish its own performance, that affidavit was enough to raise a triable issue of fact requiring a trial rather than a summary disposition, and the court reversed the judgment, denied summary judgment, and awarded costs to the sublessees. The decision is a useful corrective for commercial sublessors who assume a tenant's unpaid rent makes summary judgment close to automatic. New York's performance requirement for breach-of-contract plaintiffs has real teeth even in an ordinary rent-collection case, and a landlord's lapse on a comparatively minor ancillary obligation, like splitting a utility bill or keeping gas service connected, can become the centerpiece of a tenant's defense years later. For sublessors and master tenants managing multi-tenant commercial buildings, the practical lesson is to keep clean records of compliance with every obligation the sublease imposes on the landlord side, not just rent collection on the tenant side, and to expect that a hearing or live testimony at the trial-court level offers no protection on appeal if a genuine factual dispute should have gone to a jury instead of being resolved summarily.
live-320: The Michigan Court of Appeals has affirmed a $411,131.50 arbitration award against a commercial tenant that abandoned a Detroit retail space after the city flagged it for code violations, holding that the tenant, not the landlord, bore the contractual risk of bringing the premises into compliance. The decision in Trucks Rx, Inc. v. Padilla Investments, LLC rejects the tenant's bid to vacate the award and leaves intact a judgment that reaches the tenant's principals personally through their lease guaranties. Padilla Investments, LLC owns a commercial building in Detroit that had previously operated as a hardware store. In February 2022, Trucks Rx, Inc. and an affiliated company, Jana Trucking Line, Inc., signed a three-year commercial lease for the space to sell tires, with their principals personally guaranteeing the lease. The lease required the tenants to take the premises "as is," to comply with all applicable laws and ordinances at their own expense, and to use the property only for selling new vehicle tires. Within months of taking possession, the City of Detroit inspected the property and issued a correction order citing property-maintenance and zoning violations, followed by an emergency correction order finding the use itself was unpermitted. By July 2022 the tenants had stopped paying rent, and an August 2022 inspection found the building operating illegally as an auto-repair and truck-storage site when its only legal use was retail. The core problem was the absence of a required automatic sprinkler system, which the tenants estimated would cost more than $60,000 and take four to six months to install. The landlord's principal offered to meet with city officials alongside the tenant to resolve the issue, but the tenant did not attend, and the tenants abandoned the premises in September 2022. Padilla Investments sued for breach of contract, and the parties agreed to resolve the dispute in arbitration. The arbitrator found the tenants breached the lease by stopping rent payments and vacating the premises, ruling that the lease unambiguously placed responsibility for code compliance on the tenants, who had accepted the property "as is" and agreed to perform any work needed to operate their business lawfully. The arbitrator rejected the tenants' argument that the lease was void or unenforceable, awarded Padilla Investments $411,131.50 plus interest, and held the tenants' principals personally liable under their guaranties. The trial court confirmed the award, and the tenants appealed. Applying the deferential standard that governs judicial review of arbitration awards, the Court of Appeals held the arbitrator neither exceeded his authority nor committed a clear legal error in reading the lease to assign the sprinkler-system obligation to the tenants rather than the landlord. The panel found the "as is" and compliance clauses unambiguous and rejected the tenants' argument that the sprinkler requirement amounted to a mutual mistake justifying rescission. For commercial landlords, the decision confirms that a well-drafted "as is" clause paired with a use-compliance covenant can shift the cost of an unanticipated code requirement onto the tenant, even where the landlord made no representation about the space's readiness for the tenant's specific use and the fix is expensive. Tenants and their counsel should treat this as a caution against signing a narrow-use lease for raw or formerly differently-used space without first confirming, through diligence or a landlord work letter, who bears the cost if the intended use triggers new life-safety or zoning requirements, since an arbitrator's reading of that allocation will get heavy deference on judicial review. Lenders and guarantors should also note how quickly the dispute reached beyond the corporate tenant: the personal guaranties here converted a lease default into six-figure personal liability for the tenants' principals.
live-321: A Cook County judge has ordered real estate investor Sean Conlon to pay more than $10 million to resolve breach-of-contract litigation brought by lender Alecko Capital over the long-vacant former Rainforest Cafe building in Chicago's River North neighborhood. The ruling, issued October 20, 2026 by Judge Jerry A. Esrig of the Circuit Court of Cook County, closes out roughly a year of litigation that began when Alecko sued over a defaulted $8.3 million loan Conlon had personally guaranteed. The 22,000-square-foot freestanding building at 605 N. Clark Street has sat empty since August 2020, when the Rainforest Cafe that had anchored the corner since 1997 closed for good amid the pandemic. A venture led by Conlon had bought the property in 2015 for about $13.7 million. With the building vacant and generating no rental income, the loan secured against it became increasingly difficult to service, and Alecko Capital, the private credit and real estate investment firm led by Alex Pissios, sued in October 2025 to enforce Conlon's personal guaranty after he defaulted. The building's post-closure history has been complicated by a failed plan to lease the space to a cannabis dispensary, which collapsed after Illinois's buffer-zone rules barring a dispensary within 1,500 feet of an existing shop proved to be an obstacle, further delaying any path to re-tenanting the property and restoring cash flow against the debt. Litigation over the loan proceeded for roughly a year before Judge Esrig's October 20 order, which required Conlon to pay more than $10 million -- a figure that reflects not just the original $8.3 million principal but the default interest, fees, and costs that typically accumulate once a commercial loan goes into default and a lender is forced to litigate to collect. The case illustrates why lenders routinely structure acquisition and bridge loans on commercial property with full-recourse personal guaranties: a guaranty converts a secured, asset-level risk into unsecured personal liability extending well beyond the property's own value, and the gap between an $8.3 million loan and a $10 million-plus judgment shows how quickly default interest and litigation costs can widen that exposure once a dispute goes to judgment rather than settling early. It is also a reminder of the particular risk profile of a single-tenant, single-use commercial building that loses its anchor tenant -- once the Rainforest Cafe closed, the property had no income stream to service its debt, and each failed attempt at re-tenanting extended the period during which the loan sat unserviced. The practical lesson cuts in several directions. A commercial borrower who personally guarantees acquisition or bridge financing should treat any payment default as an immediate priority rather than something to resolve on its own timeline, since lenders are frequently entitled to accelerate the full balance, impose default interest, and add their litigation costs to the amount owed well before a borrower's refinancing plans can materialize. An owner of a single-tenant specialty property, such as a freestanding restaurant building, should build contingency plans for an extended vacancy into underwriting and loan covenants from the outset, since re-tenanting such a space can take years and can be derailed by unrelated regulatory obstacles like zoning buffer requirements for a replacement use. And for a lender, the case underscores the value of a well-documented, broadly worded personal guaranty, which is frequently the difference between recovering a secured loan's face value and recovering a judgment that also captures the accumulated cost of the default itself.
live-322: A California appeals court has reversed a $12,245,108.42 judgment against the current and former owners of a Los Angeles-area industrial site, holding that a downgradient neighbor's reliance on an environmental consultant's contamination report was not enough to establish liability as a matter of law. The decision, Joseph F. Farivar Investment Group, Inc. v. The dispute traces back decades. Before 1989, the Nardon Manufacturing Company operated a metal-fabrication facility at the Vineburn property, discharging 1,4-dioxane and other industrial solvents into onsite clarifiers and, according to the complaint, into the municipal sewer system. Meruelo Maddux Properties-1919 Vineburn Street, LLC owned the property from roughly 2005 to 2013, after which HPC Vineburn, LLC took over. The Los Angeles Regional Water Quality Control Board has overseen cleanup of a related site on the downgradient Farivar property since 2000, and in 2018 directed Vineburn to investigate further. A 2020 subsurface report by Vineburn's own consultant, Hazard Management Consulting, concluded that contamination at the Nardon facility had contributed to the dioxane and solvent plume beneath the Farivar property, identifying a contamination hot-spot near a former wastewater clarifier. Farivar Investment Group, Inc., which owns the Valley Boulevard property, and Bordan Shoe Company, Inc., which leases it, sued for continuing nuisance, continuing trespass, negligence, and declaratory relief. Leaning heavily on the 2020 consultant report and on experts who put the cost of remediating the Farivar property at roughly $11.78 million and loss-of-use damages at just under $193,000, the plaintiffs moved for and won summary adjudication on all four causes of action. On negligence, the panel held that the plaintiffs failed to establish, as a matter of law, that the defendants breached any common-law or statutory duty of care -- the consultant's factual findings about where contamination originated did not, by themselves, resolve the separate legal question of duty. On continuing nuisance and continuing trespass, the court found the plaintiffs had used an improper damages measure for what are, by their nature, continuing torts, meaning the record did not support summary adjudication on those theories either. And on the declaratory relief claim, the court held the trial court erred in partially adjudicating the issue by summary procedure. The result: the entire $12.2 million judgment is gone, and the case returns to the Los Angeles County Superior Court for further proceedings. The case also underscores how contamination liability can attach across a chain of ownership. HPC Vineburn did not create the contamination -- it inherited the site, and the site's problems, from Meruelo Maddux, which in turn inherited them from the original manufacturer. Successor owners of industrial and former-industrial parcels remain exposed to continuing-tort theories brought by neighbors long after the polluting operations have ceased, even where the current owner has, as the opinion notes, set aside funds and proposed its own cleanup plan. For commercial owners, lenders, and counsel, the ruling is a reminder not to assume a consultant's causation finding settles the legal question of duty, since negligence still requires proof of a breached standard of care and summary judgment is a demanding vehicle for getting there; that continuing nuisance and continuing trespass claims demand the right damages framework, since getting the measure wrong can doom an otherwise well-supported claim even where the underlying facts are largely undisputed; that buyers of industrial and formerly industrial property should scrutinize upgradient and downgradient parcels in diligence, since successor liability for legacy contamination can persist for decades and migrate with groundwater regardless of who currently holds title; and that tenants with any exposure to a landlord's environmental history should track litigation like this closely, since the outcome of a landlord's contamination dispute can directly affect occupancy costs, remediation access, and lease continuity.
live-323: The Ohio Court of Appeals for the Eighth Appellate District has taken the unusual step of vacating its own, three-month-old decision and issuing a new one that hands the City of Westlake a win it did not get the first time around. Crocker Park is a mixed-use development in Westlake, Ohio, combining retail, restaurants, offices, apartments, and green space across multiple contiguous parcels. Critically, the City accepted the land subject to the Declaration's existing covenants, making Westlake an Owner within the development's governance structure like any private landholder. Market Square opened in 2015, and Crocker Park Management, L.L.C., a Crocker Park subsidiary acting as the project's exclusive property manager and leasing agent, operated and maintained it for the City under a separate Operation and Maintenance Agreement, fronting out-of-pocket costs when Market Square's own revenues fell short. The City terminated that arrangement in December 2023. What followed was a lawsuit covering several intertwined disputes: how Common Area expenses should be allocated between Crocker Park and the City as a fellow Owner, counterclaims by Westlake alleging slander of title and abuse of process against Crocker Park and its manager, and a fight over whether Crocker Park properly preserved -- or instead let lapse -- a contractual right of first refusal tied to the development. The trial court had granted Crocker Park and Crocker Park Management partial summary judgment on multiple fronts, including defeating Westlake's slander-of-title and abuse-of-process counterclaims and declaring that Crocker Park had not waived its right of first refusal. Westlake appealed, and in July 2026 the Eighth District issued its first decision affirming in part and reversing in part. The panel then reconsidered. In the opinion it released October 22, 2026, authored by Presiding Judge Eileen T. Gallagher and expressly vacating the July 30 decision, the court reaffirmed the rulings in Crocker Park's favor on the slander-of-title and abuse-of-process counterclaims. But on the right of first refusal, the panel changed course: it held that Crocker Park failed to exercise the right within a reasonable time, and that the trial court therefore erred in declaring Crocker Park had not waived it. That piece of the case now returns to the trial court for further proceedings. Once Westlake accepted the Market Square parcel subject to the Declaration, it took on the same contractual rights and obligations as any private Owner, including the ability to bring and defend against ordinary common-law claims like slander of title and abuse of process, while also becoming subject to the Declarant's contractual rights, like the right of first refusal now back in play. For developers, municipal real estate counsel, and asset managers, the case is a reminder that rights of first refusal and similar contractual options frequently carry an implied reasonable-time requirement for exercise even without an express deadline in the governing document, and that delay can waive the right regardless of good intentions. Governments that accept conveyed land inside a master-planned development should expect to step fully into the shoes of a private Owner under the controlling CC&Rs, gaining enforcement rights but also assuming cost-sharing and procedural obligations. Declarants and development managers overseeing multi-owner common-area arrangements should document the timing of every option exercise and maintenance decision carefully, and parties who win at the Court of Appeals should not treat that win as final until the window for reconsideration has closed, since this case shows a panel can and will revisit its own decision when persuaded it got a discrete issue wrong.

The opinion was issued as unpublished under Colorado Appellate Rule 35(e), so it is not binding precedent in Colorado. It can still guide how trial courts read similar TI-credit provisions. BusinessDen described the result as a loss for The John Buck Co., which it identifies as the landlord. The remand will decide what, if anything, the tenant owes once the credit is applied as the panel directed, and how the eviction and fee awards are affected. Landlords should make sure TI allowance and rent-credit provisions state exactly which conditions must be met before a credit offsets rent. If lien waivers or draw packages are meant to be conditions, the lease should say that about the credit itself and not only about the cash disbursement. Tenants with large build-outs should document project completion and give the written notice the lease requires before they treat a credit as self-executing. Both sides should keep in mind that a trial win on a disputed credit can come apart on appeal, and an eviction that rests on that win carries the same risk.
live-325: In December 2023, the Law Offices of Jason W. Estavillo, P.C. signed a 66-month lease for 7,755 square feet in Suite 1280 at 555 12th Street in downtown Oakland, owned by USPA City Center, LLC. The tenant missed the settlement payments, and the landlord asked for judgment in April 2025. At a July 2025 evidentiary hearing, a Cushman & Wakefield broker qualified as an expert. He found the landlord could not mitigate while the tenant was still in the space, and he discounted the outer end of the expert's estimate. Post-judgment, the tenant got a stay and remained in the premises while paying rent. Writing for the First District, Justice Richman held that substantial evidence supported the award. The court found the expert's opinion grounded in market data, not speculation, so it passed the Sargon reliability standard. It also held that the stipulation was not an unlawful liquidated-damages penalty: it did not increase damages beyond what the lease and Civil Code section 1951.2 provide, and the tenant offered no evidence that the clause was unreasonable when signed. The court declined to consider a double-recovery argument first raised in the reply brief, which was based on rent the tenant paid during the stay, and left any offset claim for enforcement proceedings. The opinion was first filed as unpublished on September 21, 2026, and was certified for publication on October 19, 2026. It now binds California trial courts on these issues. For commercial landlords, the case is a guide to proving future rent after a tenant defaults: expert broker testimony, comparable time-on-market data for similar suites, building-level occupancy trends, and evidence of physical features that make the space hard to re-let. For tenants, it shows the cost of answering a detailed mitigation case with argument alone. It also shows that a settlement stipulating to future rent will be enforced when it matches what the lease and statute already allow.
live-326: Port Washington, a lakeshore city north of Milwaukee, approved a tax incremental district in 2025 to support Vantage Data Centers' planned $15 billion AI campus being built for Oracle and OpenAI. That district carries $458 million in local incentives. For developers and lenders, the practical point is that TIF support in Port Washington now carries election risk for any project above the $10 million threshold, which covers most industrial, data center and large mixed-use deals. Sponsors underwriting incentive-dependent projects there should build a referendum into the timeline and the capital stack, and those watching other Wisconsin municipalities should expect similar petitions where data center opposition is organized. Because the dismissal rests largely on ripeness, a future plaintiff with a specific project actually blocked by the ordinance could bring a fresh challenge, and the appellate courts may yet weigh in on whether a referendum can be layered onto the state's TID procedure.
live-327: Vantage Data Centers, based in Denver, is developing the Lighthouse campus in Port Washington, Wisconsin, a roughly $15 billion project for Oracle and OpenAI. As described in reporting on the case, the plan calls for four data centers on about 672 acres along Interstate 43, totaling some 2.5 million square feet. The first phase would draw about 1.3 gigawatts of power, with potential growth to 3.5 gigawatts, and the project would fill about 4.7 acres of wetlands. The DNR issued permits for the project on June 12, 2026. On July 10, Midwest Environmental Advocates sued the agency on behalf of the Sierra Club in Ozaukee County Circuit Court, arguing that the Wisconsin Environmental Policy Act required a full environmental impact statement for a development of this scale. The groups relied on public records showing that a DNR attorney told Vantage in July 2025 that an impact statement would be needed, and on later internal messages suggesting the company viewed that requirement as a serious threat to the project. Vantage was not a defendant; the DNR declined to comment while the case was pending, and Vantage said at the time that it had worked with the agency transparently. By January 31, 2028, the DNR must study a base case of current and projected AI data center and energy build-out in Wisconsin and its direct, indirect and cumulative effects on air and water quality, climate, water use, wetlands, wildlife, agriculture, cultural resources, energy and the economy. The Sierra Club said it expects full impact statements for specific proposals when warranted and does not view the statewide study as a substitute.
