For other Wisconsin data center sponsors, the 2028 analysis is a coming variable; its findings on cumulative water, wetland and power impacts could become the record that regulators and opponents cite when the next large campus seeks permits, so diligence and schedule assumptions should account for it.
live-328: Exit 4A is a new I-93 interchange serving Derry and Londonderry that the New Hampshire Department of Transportation, the two towns and the Federal Highway Administration have pursued for roughly 40 years. To build it and related improvements along the Folsom Road corridor in Derry, NHDOT acquired portions of private land by eminent domain, including land held by 101 Franklin Derry, LLC and S&L Elm Street Holdings, LLC, two companies owned and run by a local land developer. Those companies challenged the takings in State v. 101 Franklin Derry, LLC, et al. Their theory was that the interchange was designed mainly to benefit Woodmont Commons, a large mixed-use development in Londonderry, at the expense of Derry property owners and taxpayers. The state answered that the interchange addresses long-standing traffic and safety problems and supports economic growth in both towns, and that any advantage to a private development is incidental. The case went to a four-day jury trial. Jurors were asked whether NHDOT had shown, more likely than not, that the acquisitions serve a qualifying public use, that they are reasonably necessary and reasonable in scope, and that the project will yield a net public benefit after weighing business displacement, lost tax revenue and harm to the community. After about an hour of deliberation, the jury answered yes to all three. The trial judge, who is not named in the reporting, said an order consistent with the verdict will issue. The Attorney General's office announced the result on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. None of the coverage reports a compensation figure or whether the condemnees will appeal. The project's cost has grown well past early estimates. According to NHDOT figures cited by the Eagle-Tribune, the overall estimate is now $161.3 million across six smaller projects, including a $33.4 million Folsom Road expansion and a tunnel for the Derry Rail Trail that the state agreed to build in a separate federal settlement earlier this year. Derry and Londonderry have each committed $5 million. The Folsom Road phase is expected to be finished in summer 2028, when the interchange is expected to open, with remaining work running into the early 2030s. The Eagle-Tribune noted that the verdict does not resolve every issue around the project. For owners and developers, the verdict underscores that a public-use challenge to a highway taking faces long odds once a project has a long planning record and an evident traffic purpose, even when a nearby private development will plainly gain from the new access. The net-benefit question New Hampshire puts to juries does let a condemnee put business displacement and lost tax base in front of the factfinder, but it did not carry the day here. Owners facing takings for infrastructure that also serves private growth should weigh whether resources are better spent documenting severance damages, access changes and business losses for the compensation phase, and developers relying on new public access should track condemnation challenges as a schedule risk.
live-329: In September 2023, Sound Development Group LLC proposed a commercial and residential project in downtown Oak Harbor, next to Hal Ramaley Memorial Park: a one-story brewpub with single-story residential units. The city turned that plan down and asked for something denser. The developer came back with a four-story Home2 Suites by Hilton with 107 rooms and meeting space. Its parking lot would extend onto part of the park. At the time, the city code required voters to approve any sale of developed park property. According to the opinion, city planning staff gave the developer several options: hold an election, drop the fourth floor, cut the pool and other amenities to free up parking, or amend the code. The parties pursued the amendment. At an August 13, 2024 public hearing, the city council passed Ordinance 1999 by a six-to-one vote. It allows park property to be sold or traded without a vote if the council approves a development agreement and finds that the exchange meets set land-area and market-value tests, or that the private party's park improvements are worth at least 150 percent of the land conveyed. The city's planner told the council the change was prompted by the hotel proposal. Whidbey Environmental Action Network sued on August 30, 2024. It argued the city violated SEPA by passing the ordinance without first reviewing its environmental impacts. The trial court granted summary judgment to the city on May 1, 2025, ruling that the ordinance was not an action covered by SEPA and was categorically exempt in any event. Division One reversed. Writing for the panel, Acting Chief Judge Bowman held that Ordinance 1999 is a nonproject action under WAC 197-11-704(2)(b)(i). Its conditions tie the transfer of park land to a specific purpose, development, and so they control the use or modification of the environment, much as a zoning ordinance does. The court rejected the city's position that review could wait until a sale or development was actually proposed. It noted that a concrete proposal already existed, with site plans, floor plans, landscaping plans and renderings showing the parking lot. The court also held that the procedural-action exemption in WAC 197-11-800(19) does not apply, because the ordinance contains substantive standards. The case goes back to the trial court for further proceedings. For hotel and mixed-use developers, the decision shows a timing risk. When a project needs a code amendment or a public-land deal, the amendment itself can be the trigger for SEPA review, and skipping it gives opponents a way to stall the project. The safer course is to run the environmental threshold determination on the enabling legislation alongside the project application, using the plans already submitted, so an ordinance passed for one project does not later become the target of a lawsuit.
live-330: Valcourt Building Services of Georgia, L.C. had a contract with the owner of a commercial building to provide exterior maintenance, including pressure washing the rooftop cooling-tower fans. BSC Realty Services, LLC managed the building. Valcourt subcontracted the fan cleaning to a separate maintenance company. In the contract, Valcourt agreed to defend and indemnify both the owner and BSC against injury claims arising from its work or its subcontractors' work. The only exception was liability arising from the sole negligence of the owner or manager. On October 7, 2021, the subcontractor's worker checked in with the building's engineers, who worked for a BSC affiliate. They confirmed that power to the first fan was off, and he cleaned it. After they confirmed power was off to a second fan, he climbed a ladder, held a blade with one hand and began washing. He heard a click, the fan began to turn, and he fell and was seriously injured. The engineers could shut fans down either through the building automation system or at a locked rooftop electrical room. Only the electrical room allowed a federal lockout/tagout procedure. The worker's expert testified that cutting power through the automation system alone did not properly de-energize the fan. The worker sued several defendants, including BSC. BSC filed a third-party claim against Valcourt for breach of contract and indemnification. The trial court granted summary judgment to Valcourt, finding that any liability came from the sole negligence of the owner's or manager's engineers. Valcourt also argued that BSC's appeal was untimely. The appeals court disagreed: no civil case disposition form had been filed, so no final judgment was entered under OCGA 9-11-58(b), the order remained interlocutory, and the trial court could vacate and re-enter it. On the merits, Presiding Judge McFadden's opinion for the Fourth Division found no direct evidence of whether the fan had power when the worker fell. The automation logs had not been kept. The circumstantial evidence pointed both ways. The click suggested power was restored, but other evidence showed the fan makes little or no noise when re-energized, water pressure from a power washer alone can turn the blades, and a co-worker saw the blades slowing after the fall. A jury could reasonably find that water, not electricity, moved the fan. Because of that dispute, Valcourt could not show as a matter of law that the sole-negligence exception applied, so the summary judgment was reversed. The court did not reach BSC's separate argument about Valcourt's training of the worker. For owners and property managers, the takeaways are practical. Indemnity clauses that exclude only the indemnitee's sole negligence are valuable, but they are decided on causation facts, so documents matter. Written lockout/tagout procedures, preserving building-system logs after an incident, and records showing which party controlled each step of a shutdown can decide whether the risk lands on the contractor or on the building's own insurers.
live-331: Colliers International NY LLC sued City Hall Commons LLC in Supreme Court, New York County, to collect a commission for a lease renewal between the landlord and a tenant that is not a party to the case. The decision does not identify the property. The September 2019 renewal agreement stated that Colliers was the exclusive broker for the transaction and that the landlord would pay the broker fees. The landlord moved to dismiss under CPLR 3211. It argued there was no binding agreement or privity between it and Colliers, and it relied on its refusal to sign a separate brokerage agreement after the renewal was done. Justice Debra A. James converted the motion to one for summary judgment under CPLR 3211(c), denied the landlord's motion, and granted the broker's cross-motion in an order entered on or about September 10, 2024. A money judgment of $307,326.18 was entered on January 31, 2025. A First Department panel of Justices Scarpulla, González, Rodriguez, Rosado and O'Neill Levy unanimously affirmed on October 22, 2026. The court relied on its own precedent, including Newmark & Co. Real Estate Inc. v. 2615 E. 17 St. Realty LLC and Helmsley-Spear, Inc. v. New York Blood Center, Inc. It held that when an agreement between a landlord and a tenant names the plaintiff as exclusive broker and says the landlord will pay its commission, that statement, backed by other documents, entitles the broker to the commission as a matter of law. The renewal agreement directly contradicted the landlord's no-privity argument. Emails between Colliers and the landlord's representative also showed Colliers' role in the negotiations. The panel also rejected the argument that refusing to sign a later brokerage agreement cancelled the obligation. Once the landlord had agreed in the renewal to pay the fee, it could not undo that by declining further paperwork. The court considered the landlord's other arguments and found them unavailing. For owners, the practical point is that broker clauses in leases and renewals are not boilerplate. If a landlord does not intend to pay a particular broker, or wants the fee subject to a separate agreement with conditions, the lease should say so. Signing a renewal that names an exclusive broker and assigns the fee to the landlord can make the landlord liable for the commission even if it never signs a brokerage contract. For brokers, the decision supports keeping the emails and other records of their role in negotiations, along with the lease language, as proof that they earned the fee.
live-332: A federal judge in the Western District of Washington has denied Yardi Systems, Inc.'s motion for summary judgment in a proposed class action accusing the property-management software vendor of enabling an illegal rent-fixing scheme among multifamily landlords, clearing the way for the case to proceed through a broader round of discovery. The October 13 ruling, issued by U.S. District Judge Robert S. Lasnik in Duffy v. Yardi Systems, Inc., No. 2:23-cv-01391, is the latest in a string of setbacks for Yardi since the suit was filed in September 2023. The case, brought by named plaintiffs McKenna Duffy and Michael Brett on behalf of a proposed nationwide class of renters, centers on Yardi's RENTmaximizer product, later rebranded as Revenue IQ. Plaintiffs allege the software ingested non-public pricing, occupancy, and lease-term data from competing landlords who licensed the platform, then used that pooled information to recommend rents back to each landlord-client, effectively functioning as a hub for horizontal price coordination among competitors who would otherwise set rents independently. The theory echoes algorithmic-pricing antitrust claims that have proliferated against RealPage, Yardi's larger rival in the revenue-management software market, in separate multidistrict litigation pending in the Middle District of Tennessee. Judge Lasnik's order is procedural rather than a merits verdict, but it is significant because of what it declines to do: end the case before a jury or further fact-finding can test the plaintiffs' theory. In denying summary judgment, the court found that segmented discovery, an earlier arrangement pausing broader fact-finding against the dismissed landlord-defendants while the parties developed the Yardi-specific record, did not eliminate the need for a fuller discovery record before the remaining claims could be resolved. The order also sealed certain Yardi confidential business information from the public docket and denied both sides' competing motions to exclude expert testimony. The ruling builds on two earlier defeats for Yardi. In December 2024, Judge Lasnik denied the company's motion to dismiss outright, holding that the plaintiffs had plausibly alleged a per se unlawful antitrust conspiracy, a notable holding because per se treatment dispenses with the more exacting burden plaintiffs otherwise face under the antitrust rule of reason. In March 2026, the court trimmed the case on jurisdictional grounds, dismissing ten out-of-state landlord co-defendants, among them Banyan Living Ohio LLC, Envolve Communities LLC, Grubb Properties LLC, Habitat Co. LLC, and McWhinney Property Management LLC, for lack of personal jurisdiction in Washington, leaving Yardi as the central remaining defendant. For commercial real estate owners and operators, the case is a reminder that legal exposure from algorithmic revenue-management software does not run only to the handful of vendors, such as RealPage, that have drawn the most public attention. Any multifamily owner or manager licensing a platform that relies on pooled, non-public competitor data to generate pricing recommendations faces the same basic antitrust theory. In practice, that means auditing existing revenue-management vendor contracts and data-sharing arrangements for how pricing recommendations use pooled competitor data, tracking the growing patchwork of state and local algorithmic-pricing ordinances in markets where a company operates, and watching closely how the per se versus rule-of-reason question is ultimately resolved on the merits, since it will shape antitrust exposure well beyond this particular case.
live-333: A commercial building owner's fight to recover $2.7 million for years of water and salt damage is back on, after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed a federal district court's summary judgment in favor of the owner's property insurer. The October 16, 2026 ruling in Industrial Park Center LLC v. Great Northern Insurance Co. turns on a question that matters well beyond this one claim: when is property damage "fortuitous," and therefore covered by an all-risk policy, versus an uninsurable certainty the owner should have expected. The Arizona Supreme Court answered that question for the first time just weeks earlier, at the Ninth Circuit's request, and the new standard it set now governs every comparable claim in the state. Industrial Park Center LLC, doing business as Mainspring Capital Group, owns a commercial building in Tempe, Arizona that it leased to a fish-processing tenant and insured under an all-risk commercial property policy issued by Great Northern Insurance Company. Over several years, the building suffered recurring water and salt intrusion. According to court filings, an engineering firm Mainspring retained, MBJ, had recommended specific preventive measures, a waterproof floor coating, a vapor barrier, and additional drainage systems, that were never installed. When Mainspring submitted a claim for roughly $2.7 million in resulting damage, Great Northern denied it, arguing the loss was not fortuitous: because the damage was reasonably foreseeable and effectively certain to occur without those preventive measures, the insurer argued, it fell outside what an all-risk policy is meant to cover in the first place. Mainspring sued in Maricopa County Superior Court in 2022; Great Northern removed the case to the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona on diversity jurisdiction. In July 2024, the district court granted Great Northern summary judgment, applying the Ninth Circuit's existing fortuity test from Ingenco, which asks whether a loss was reasonably foreseeable and almost certain to occur. The court found Mainspring's loss met that description and was therefore not fortuitous, and later awarded Great Northern roughly $198,234 in attorneys' fees. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit concluded Arizona law did not yet resolve what fortuitous means in this context and, in late 2025, certified the question to the Arizona Supreme Court. The Arizona Supreme Court answered on September 1, 2026, in an opinion by Justice Clint Bolick, rejecting the stricter foreseeability-based test the district court had used. Instead, the court adopted a subjective, knowledge-based standard, drawing on the Restatement (First) of Contracts: a loss is fortuitous, and therefore insurable, unless the insured actually knew, at the time the policy was issued, that the damage had already occurred, was already in progress, or was certain to occur. Foreseeability alone, even strong foreseeability, is not enough to strip a loss of coverage under this standard. Applying it, the Ninth Circuit's October 16 memorandum disposition reversed the district court's summary judgment and remanded, reviving Mainspring's breach-of-contract and bad-faith claims against Great Northern for further proceedings. The decision is unpublished and therefore not binding Ninth Circuit precedent, but the Arizona Supreme Court ruling it applies is now the controlling statement of Arizona insurance law on fortuity. For commercial property owners, the practical stakes are significant: all-risk policies are the backbone of CRE lenders' insurance requirements, and insurers frequently resist claims tied to a known, long-deferred maintenance or design problem by arguing the eventual failure was predictable and therefore not a fortuitous, insurable event. Arizona's new rule narrows that defense considerably, since an insurer can no longer defeat coverage merely by showing the loss was statistically likely or even almost certain absent repairs; it must show the owner actually knew, when the policy was purchased or renewed, that the damage had already happened, was already underway, or was a sure thing. Owners who have deferred an engineer's or contractor's recommended fix should not assume that deferral forfeits coverage if the predicted failure eventually occurs, though they should be cautious about what internal reports and engineering assessments say about the certainty of an outcome, since those documents will be the first thing an insurer's coverage counsel examines in any future claim, and lenders and asset managers overseeing assets with known deferred-maintenance issues in Arizona, or in another state that may look to this decision as persuasive authority on a question many states have not yet resolved, should confirm their insurance placement and claims strategy account for this more owner-favorable standard.
live-334: A Cook County judge has cleared the way for a special servicer to take title to Illinois Center, the twin-tower office complex at 111 E. Wacker Drive and 233 N. Michigan Avenue in Chicago's East Loop, after ruling against the AmTrust RE affiliate that has owned the roughly 2.1-million-square-foot property since 2015. The ruling sets up a Cook County sheriff's sale on November 12, 2026, and marks one of the more dramatic value collapses yet documented in Chicago's distressed office market. Cook County Associate Judge Edward Robles ruled against the AmTrust RE affiliate in September 2026, entering a judgment of foreclosure on the $260 million commercial mortgage-backed securities loan secured by the complex. According to The Real Deal, Bisnow, and other trade-press accounts published October 19 and 20, 2026, AmTrust had stopped actively contesting the case over the summer, declining to oppose the lender's motion for summary judgment after workout talks with special servicer LNR Partners, LLC broke down. With the judgment entered, the Cook County sheriff's office has scheduled a public auction of the property for November 12, and LNR Partners, acting on behalf of the CMBS trust's bondholders, is positioned to submit the winning credit bid and take title. The loan dates to 2015, when the AmTrust RE affiliate acquired the Illinois Center towers and financed the purchase with the $260 million CMBS loan, then underwritten against a $390 million valuation. The borrower fell behind on payments, and LNR Partners filed a foreclosure suit in the Circuit Court of Cook County's Chancery Division. By the time Judge Robles entered judgment, the numbers behind the loan had deteriorated sharply: Morningstar Credit data cited in the reporting puts the property's most recent appraisal at just $66 million, an 83% drop from the 2015 origination value and a 22% decline from an already-reduced 2024 appraisal. Occupancy at the complex had fallen to roughly 33% as of the end of 2025, according to servicer commentary described in the coverage. For a property once counted among the signature assets of Chicago's East Loop skyline, part of the Illinois Center development built in the architectural idiom associated with Mies van der Rohe, the scale of the write-down illustrates how far the city's office downturn has progressed for aging, undercapitalized towers built on pre-pandemic rent and occupancy assumptions. The case also follows a now-familiar pattern for CMBS special servicers handling distressed Chicago office loans: rather than pursue an extended workout or loan modification, LNR Partners appears set to take the property into real-estate-owned status directly through the sheriff's sale process, giving the servicer and bondholders direct control over any future repositioning, lease-up, or disposition strategy rather than continuing to negotiate with a borrower that has effectively walked away. For other Chicago-area office owners facing CMBS loans originated in the mid-2010s at valuations that no longer reflect current market realities, the Illinois Center matter is a useful and cautionary data point. A borrower who stops contesting foreclosure once it becomes clear that remaining equity has been wiped out, as AmTrust appears to have done here, can move a case to judgment and sale relatively quickly once summary judgment goes unopposed; special servicers and bondholders, in turn, appear increasingly willing to take title outright through a credit bid rather than extend further forbearance on assets whose appraised values have fallen this far below outstanding debt. Owners and lenders alike should watch Cook County sheriff's sale calendars and servicer commentary for a read on how quickly comparable downtown Chicago office towers are moving from default to disposition, since the timeline here, a foreclosure suit in late 2024 to judgment and sale by November 2026, may be a useful benchmark.
live-335: A lawsuit that has worked its way through Goochland County, Virginia's circuit court since December 2025 reached a significant hearing on October 20, 2026, putting the county's process for approving a data-center-friendly zoning overlay to its most direct test yet. The case, filed by four Goochland property owners against the county, its Board of Supervisors, and its Planning Commission, asks the court to void the Technology Overlay District that supervisors approved in a 4-1 vote in November 2025 -- a zoning measure covering roughly 4,400 acres, about 3,500 of them inside the county's West Creek Business Park, that allows data centers, pharmaceutical companies, and biomedical researchers to locate there by right. The dispute matters beyond Goochland's borders because it tests, in a Virginia courtroom, a legal theory that has become increasingly common as communities push back against data-center construction: that a locality's zoning process itself, not just the land use it ultimately authorizes, can be unwound in court if the locality cuts procedural corners on the way to a contentious vote. The plaintiffs' core claim is that Goochland County violated Virginia law in the process it used to adopt the TOD. According to reporting on the case, the plaintiffs allege that county officials failed to properly identify all of the properties affected by the overlay before the board's vote, and that the ordinance supervisors ultimately adopted differed from the version described in the public notices that preceded it. The plaintiffs have also pointed to last-minute changes made to the measure the same night the board voted to approve it. The litigation has already produced one notable procedural skirmish. The county initially sought to have the full legislative record underlying the TOD vote, reported at roughly 8,500 pages, entered into the case, arguing it could not know which portions might become relevant until the plaintiffs' specific objections were clarified. In late May 2026, Circuit Court Judge Timothy Sanner rejected that approach and instead directed the county to produce a narrower, revised set of TOD-related records. The county separately set aside a $250,000 legal defense budget to litigate the case. The case returned to court on October 20, 2026, for a hearing on the county's demurrer, the Virginia procedural vehicle roughly equivalent to a motion to dismiss. County officials have expressed public confidence the suit will be dismissed, with some reporting suggesting a ruling could come as soon as the hearing itself; no decision has been reported as of this writing. The case is a reminder to commercial real estate owners and developers that a zoning approval's practical finality is not assured the moment a board votes yes: an enactment remains vulnerable to a procedural challenge for as long as a locality's own notice-and-process requirements were arguably not followed, and such challenges can take a year or more to resolve. Data center developers who have increasingly relied on overlay districts to avoid case-by-case special-use fights should treat an overlay's procedural pedigree as a live front in community opposition strategy, and localities adopting similar overlays should make sure the adopted text matches what public notices described and avoid substantive last-night amendments -- the cost of litigating that question, as Goochland's quarter-million-dollar defense budget and year-plus of docket time show, can rival the cost of getting the process right the first time. live-336: A tenant that dismantles and hauls away structures from a commercial landlord's property has committed conversion, but that finding alone does not put a dollar figure in the landlord's pocket. The court separately held that Michelmann forfeited its tortious-interference claim by failing to support it with a developed, authority-backed argument on appeal, and that because Michelmann had elected to treat Link Media as a holdover tenant rather than a trespasser, a new lease arose on the same terms as the 1987 lease, including its year-to-year renewal structure, supporting the separate rent judgment against Link Media. The case is a compact lesson for anyone negotiating or litigating a ground lease, billboard easement, or similar arrangement where a tenant's structures sit on someone else's land. A lease's holdover provisions matter long after signing: Michelmann prevailed on its rent claim largely because its decades-old lease language kept renewing the deal on the same terms even after the named tenant disappeared through a chain of assignments. But winning the liability fight over a tenant's unauthorized removal of fixtures is not the same as collecting real money for it; a landlord who wants more than a token damages award needs proof of fair market value in hand, whether from comparable sales, replacement-cost testimony tied to depreciation, or an expert appraisal, not just a statement of what it would cost to rebuild. For tenants and assignees taking over legacy leases, the opinion is a reminder that silence about post-termination removal rights defaults against them: absent an explicit grace period, removal has to happen while possession as a tenant continues, calendared carefully, since an ambiguous or silent lease will be read against a tenant that leaves structures behind too long, and electing to treat an occupant as a holdover rather than pursuing eviction can quietly extend the original lease's terms, including rent escalators, for years beyond what either side expected.

live-338: A proposal to build a $1 billion, 460,000-square-foot data center on the edge of Urbana, Ohio has turned into a federal civil rights and zoning fight after the city passed an emergency moratorium and rezoned the developer's own land out from under its pending application. live-339: A North Carolina trial judge has ruled that a data center developer's project can proceed despite a county-wide moratorium, offering one of the first clear answers to a legal question now pending in dozens of jurisdictions across the state: does a developer who secured zoning approval before a moratorium took effect have a vested right to keep building anyway? In a summary judgment order reported September 22, 2026, Chatham County Superior Court Judge John Morris sided with the developer, ECO TIP West, LLC, finding no genuine issue of material fact and ruling that the company was entitled to judgment as a matter of law. ECO TIP West sued Chatham County in its own Superior Court on April 23, 2026, after county commissioners adopted a 12-month moratorium on new data-center development on February 11, 2026, running until February 11, 2027 or until the county adopts new data-center-specific zoning regulations, whichever comes first. North Carolina news organizations have tracked roughly 30 local governments statewide that have passed comparable moratoria amid a surge of large-scale data-center proposals. ECO TIP West argued its planned 750-megawatt data center at the Triangle Innovation Point West parcel near Moncure, part of the Moncure Megasite, was different: the company received a zoning permit for the project from the county on October 29, 2025, more than three months before the moratorium existed, giving it a statutory by-right use the county could not retroactively strip away. The company has said it had already invested more than $11 million developing the project before the county intervened. Data-center moratoria have become one of the fastest-growing categories of commercial land-use litigation nationally, as local governments from Ohio and Michigan to Georgia and Kentucky have reached for temporary building pauses against resident opposition over noise, water consumption, and grid strain. The recurring legal question in nearly every dispute is the same one Chatham County lost: whether a developer that obtained permits or approval before a moratorium's effective date holds a vested right the moratorium cannot touch. Judge Morris's ruling does not resolve that question for every project statewide, since vested-rights analysis is fact-specific, but as one of the first North Carolina trial court rulings to address it directly, with a documented permit predating the moratorium by several months, it is likely to embolden similarly situated developers while giving counties reason to scrutinize permitting status before adopting their own moratoria -- particularly given that the court ordered damages for the delay, not merely a forward-looking exemption.
live-340: The unwinding of Lurin Capital, the Dallas-based multifamily syndicator that once controlled nearly 10,000 Class-C apartment units across five Sun Belt states, has reached an unusual legal milestone: three of its lenders have asked a federal bankruptcy court to force its founder, Jon Venetos, into Chapter 7 bankruptcy against his will. Silver Point Finance, LLC, Vista Bank, and NexPoint Real Estate Finance, Inc. filed the involuntary petition on September 17, 2026, in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas, citing a combined roughly $33.7 million in judgments already entered against Venetos personally. Industry observers have called involuntary filings against an individual one of the rarest moves in bankruptcy, a reflection of how unusual it is for creditors to take this step rather than simply chasing a judgment debtor's assets individually. The petition is the latest, and in some ways the most consequential, front in a cascade of litigation that has engulfed Venetos since Lurin's multifamily portfolio began defaulting in 2025. Lurin and a succession of affiliated single-property ownership entities began filing their own Chapter 11 petitions in March 2026 to block foreclosures on individual apartment complexes, with the parent entity's broader Chapter 11 case following the next month. That corporate bankruptcy process, however, does nothing to shield Venetos from the personal guaranties he signed on Lurin's behalf, and lenders have been racing through 2026 to reduce those guaranties to judgment. Just two weeks before the involuntary petition, Acore Capital Mortgage won summary judgment against Venetos in New York Supreme Court for roughly $19 million, tied to a mezzanine loan guaranty on The Cove, a Tampa apartment complex Acore took back at a foreclosure auction after Lurin stopped paying in December 2023. The involuntary petition itself names three petitioning creditors with their own distinct judgments: Silver Point Finance holds a $22.7 million judgment for breach of a promissory note, Vista Bank holds a $3.1 million judgment, and NexPoint Real Estate Finance holds a $5 million judgment. Under the Bankruptcy Code, three or more creditors holding qualifying unsecured claims can force an individual or entity into involuntary bankruptcy if the debtor is generally not paying debts as they come due, a standard that becomes easier to satisfy once a debtor has accumulated multiple unpaid judgments across unrelated creditors, as Venetos has. The move effectively takes the question of Venetos's personal assets out of a creditor-by-creditor race to collect and puts it under the control of a bankruptcy trustee, who can marshal and liquidate whatever remains for the benefit of the full creditor pool rather than whoever executes fastest. Venetos's exposure extends well beyond the parties named in the involuntary petition. Acore's $19 million New York judgment is only one piece of litigation the lender has pursued against him; Fannie Mae has separately sued over a roughly $77 million default tied to a Houston-area loan, KeyBank has sued over Dallas apartment loan defaults, and a Dallas office landlord has pursued Venetos personally over an alleged $5.3 million lease guaranty. The FBI's Dallas field office has also opened an investigation into Venetos and Lurin, soliciting information from investors about how much they put in, what they were told the money would be used for, and what distributions, if any, they received, though no criminal charges have been filed and an open investigation does not establish wrongdoing. For commercial lenders and syndicator investors alike, the Lurin collapse has become a reference case for how quickly a sponsor's personal guaranty exposure can outpace the underlying corporate restructuring once a multifamily portfolio built on floating-rate, Sun Belt value-add bets stops cash-flowing. An involuntary Chapter 7 petition against a sponsor is rare precisely because most lenders prefer to pursue their own collateral and their own guaranty judgment rather than share a shrinking pool of personal assets with other creditors; that three separate lenders concluded a coordinated filing served them better than individual collection efforts signals how limited Venetos's remaining unencumbered assets are believed to be, particularly after a separate 2025 foreclosure on his Aspen home. Sponsors who sign personal, uncapped guaranties on aggregated portfolios of non-recourse-adjacent debt should treat this case as a concrete illustration of how a string of individually modest guaranty judgments can combine into exactly the kind of multi-creditor pressure that makes an involuntary petition feasible, while lenders holding similar guaranties should note that coordinating with other creditors, rather than racing to the courthouse alone, can be the more effective route once a guarantor's asset base is visibly shrinking.
live-341: A New York appeals court has handed commercial landlords a costly reminder about the price of skipping lease notice procedures, even when a tenant has clearly abandoned its space. On October 27, 2026, the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, First Department, unanimously affirmed the dismissal of Renaissance Midtown West LLC's lawsuit against its former office tenant, Lividini & Company, LLC, and the tenant's principal, rejecting claims for unpaid rent, breach of guaranty, and corporate veil-piercing in a single, tightly reasoned order. The underlying facts, as recounted in the opinion, trace back to August 2020, when counsel for Lividini notified the landlord that the tenant was vacating the leased premises before the end of the lease term. The landlord did not respond at the time. More than four years passed before Renaissance Midtown West commenced its action in New York County Supreme Court in November 2024, seeking rent for the balance of the lease term, enforcement of a guaranty against the tenant's principal, and an order piercing the corporate veil to hold that principal personally liable. Justice Lyle E. Frank dismissed the amended complaint on July 24, 2025, and the landlord appealed. The First Department's analysis centered on paragraph 17(1) of the lease, a conditional-limitation clause allowing the landlord to terminate for defaults other than nonpayment of rent, including if the premises became vacant or deserted, but only by first serving a five-day notice to cure specifying the default and then, if the tenant failed to cure in good faith, a three-day notice of cancellation. The court held that the tenant's early vacatur triggered the landlord's obligation to give that notice before reentering and reletting the premises, citing the Court of Appeals' decision in Holy Properties v. Cole Products. The landlord's argument that it never intended to terminate the lease under that clause, but merely wanted to collect rent still owed, did not persuade the panel: the landlord's own allegations that the tenant returned the keys without objection, and that the landlord then signed a new lease with a replacement tenant, were inconsistent with any claim that the original landlord-tenant relationship continued. The court distinguished a case the landlord relied on, 622 Third Ave. Co. LLC v. Hyatt Leader Ltd., noting that unlike the landlord there, Renaissance Midtown West never told the departing tenant that accepting the keys was without prejudice to a later damages claim, and the record showed no further communication between the parties after the tenant's 2020 notice until the lawsuit was filed in 2024. The panel separately affirmed dismissal of two additional claims that often travel alongside a landlord's rent claim. The guaranty claim failed because the form guaranty attached to the lease was blank and unexecuted, and New York's statute of frauds for guaranties, General Obligations Law section 5-701(a)(2), requires a signed writing regardless of the parties' course of dealing. The veil-piercing claim against the tenant's principal failed because, as the court explained, veil-piercing is not an independent cause of action but a set of facts and circumstances that must show the principal exercised complete domination and control over the corporation to perpetrate a wrong or injustice, under the standard set out by the Court of Appeals in Cortlandt Street Recovery Corp. v. Bonderman. A bare allegation that the principal failed to maintain a separate bank account for the tenant, the court held, falls well short. For commercial landlords, asset managers, and the in-house and outside counsel who draft and enforce their leases, the ruling underscores that the mechanics of lease notice provisions are not a formality to be worked around after the fact. A landlord that wants to preserve a damages claim after a tenant vacates early needs to serve whatever default and cancellation notices the lease requires, or at minimum state clearly and in writing, at the time it accepts the keys, that doing so is without prejudice to pursuing unpaid rent. Waiting years to sue, as happened here, only compounds the risk, since the landlord's own subsequent conduct, such as re-letting to a new tenant without any contemporaneous reservation of rights, can end up supplying the evidence that defeats its claim. The decision also serves as a check-your-forms moment: leases that attach a guaranty as a standard exhibit should be confirmed as fully executed, not left as an unsigned specimen, and a veil-piercing theory against a tenant's principal needs concrete, specific allegations of abuse of the corporate form rather than generic bookkeeping complaints.
live-342: A published decision from Washington's Court of Appeals, Division One, is giving multifamily owners and their lenders a fresh data point in the long-running fight over how far a city's rent and eviction regulations can go before they cross into a compensable taking of property. On October 26, 2026, the court reversed a trial court's dismissal of GRE Downtowner LLC's inverse condemnation claims against the City of Seattle, holding that the company pleaded enough facts about the cumulative financial impact of a series of tenant-protection ordinances to let its case proceed past the pleading stage. GRE Downtowner owns and operates Addison on Fourth, an affordable housing complex of 254 studio and one-bedroom units, 46 artist studios, and four commercial spaces near downtown Seattle. GRE Downtowner bought the property in 2012 for $12.5 million and put in another $26.5 million to qualify it for the federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program, with financing support from the Washington State Housing Finance Commission, Citigroup as bond underwriter, and Freddie Mac and East West Bank as credit enhancers. The project stabilized by 2015, and from 2015 through 2018 it ran a positive annual cash flow, collecting between roughly 90 and 94 percent of its maximum allowable rental income each year under HUD's income-based rent caps. According to the complaint, that changed as Seattle's City Council adopted a succession of tenant-protection measures beginning in 2018: the Fair Chance Housing Ordinance barring criminal-history-based tenant screening and eviction; a 2019 Roommate Ordinance extending occupancy rights to a tenant's family members and other residents; a Winter Eviction Ban; a COVID-19 eviction moratorium running from March 2020 to February 2022; and, in September 2021, both an extension of the minimum rent-increase notice period from 60 to 180 days and a new Economic Displacement Relocation Assistance ordinance requiring landlords to pay relocation costs to tenants who leave after a rent increase of 10 percent or more. GRE Downtowner alleges its maximum-rent collection rate fell from 87 percent in 2019 to just 44.1 percent in 2023, producing annual losses of $683,353 in 2020, $980,043 in 2021, $1.8 million in 2022, and $2.7 million in 2023, and leaving the property, in the company's telling, functionally valueless on an income-approach appraisal. GRE Downtowner sued the City in King County Superior Court in October 2024, asserting inverse condemnation claims for both partial and per se regulatory takings under article I, section 16 of the Washington Constitution, the state's analog to the Fifth Amendment's takings clause. The City moved to dismiss under Civil Rule 12(b)(6), and the trial court granted the motion in February 2025. After the Washington Supreme Court declined to pull the appeal up to itself, Division One took up the case and, in an opinion authored by Judge David S. Mann, reversed. Applying Washington's comparatively lenient 12(b)(6) standard, which asks only whether the plaintiff could prove any set of facts consistent with the complaint that would justify relief, the court held that GRE Downtowner's allegations about the ordinances' cumulative economic effect were legally sufficient to proceed, under the regulatory-takings framework Washington courts borrow from the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Lingle v. Chevron U.S.A. Inc. and the state's own 2023 ruling in Washington Food Industry Association v. City of Seattle. The decision does not resolve whether Seattle's ordinances actually worked a taking of GRE Downtowner's property, since that question now returns to the trial court, but it is a meaningful procedural win for owners who want a court to weigh a city's regulations by their combined effect rather than evaluate each ordinance in isolation. Lawyers advising multifamily owners facing new local tenant-protection measures should take two things from the case: document the property's financial performance before and after each new ordinance takes effect, because a cumulative-impact takings theory depends on being able to isolate and quantify the loss tied to each rule, and recognize that a stack of individually modest ordinances can still support a viable claim if the compounding effect leaves an owner with no economically viable use of the property. Lenders and investors underwriting rent-regulated or LIHTC housing in jurisdictions with an active tenant-protection agenda should watch how the case develops on remand, since it will test how far Washington courts are willing to let that theory go on the merits, while municipalities drafting new landlord-tenant rules should take note that courts are willing to look past ordinance-by-ordinance review and ask whether the regulatory scheme as a whole crossed the line.
live-343: A commercial property owner that skipped its own eminent domain trial has lost its bid on appeal to recover more than the government's pre-trial deposit for the taking. In BFT Rental, LLC v. The City filed its condemnation action against BFT on November 8, 2023, seeking to acquire an easement across BFT-owned property in Fayetteville for construction of a water-transmission main. Acting under Arkansas's quick-take statute, Ark. Code Ann. section 18-15-303, the City deposited $112,180 into the court registry and obtained an order of immediate possession on November 16, 2023, allowing it to take possession and begin the public works project while the ultimate compensation question was litigated. BFT moved to withdraw the deposited funds, which the court granted, and the case proceeded toward a jury trial on the amount of just compensation. What followed was a run of attorney transitions that proved consequential. BFT's original counsel withdrew in the spring of 2024, and replacement counsel entered an appearance that July. The circuit court set a one-day jury trial for April 30, 2025. On January 31, 2025, roughly three months before trial, that attorney also moved to withdraw. The City objected to any resulting continuance, noting the case had already been pending for well over a year, its witnesses were prepared to proceed, and this was BFT's second attorney to seek withdrawal during the litigation. The circuit court granted the withdrawal on February 27, 2025, but denied the continuance. BFT did not retain new counsel until after the trial date had passed and never objected to the February 27 ruling at the time; instead, BFT simply did not appear for the April 30 jury trial. With no appearance, no witness list, and no exhibit list from the defense, the City moved for a directed verdict, which the circuit court granted, affirming the City's ownership of the easement and fixing just compensation at the $112,180 already on deposit. The court explained in its written order that, absent any evidence from BFT, a reasonable jury would not have had a sufficient evidentiary basis to award BFT just compensation beyond that amount. On appeal, BFT argued that the circuit court abused its discretion by allowing its attorney to withdraw while denying a continuance, and that the error tainted both the directed verdict and the later denial of its motion for a new trial. The Court of Appeals never reached the merits of that argument. Citing Tate-Smith v. Cupples and Nash v. Nash, the panel held that under Arkansas's preservation doctrine, an objection raised for the first time in a motion for new trial is not timely and cannot be considered on appeal, a rule designed to prevent a litigant from waiting to see whether a gamble pays off before raising an available objection. Because BFT voiced no complaint about the February 27 ruling until two months later, after it had already lost at trial, the panel held the issue was unpreserved, and it rejected BFT's separate challenge to the denial of its new-trial motion on the same ground, also noting that BFT's briefing never argued why the directed verdict itself was substantively wrong. Eminent domain compensation disputes are almost always about the numbers, but this case is a reminder that appraisal and valuation evidence is worthless if it never reaches the jury. For commercial landlords, developers, and other property owners facing condemnation, the lesson is that a government's statutory deposit, once left undisputed by competent evidence at trial, can become the ceiling on recovery as a matter of law, and that any scheduling dispute or counsel transition close to trial needs an immediate, on-the-record objection and a formal continuance motion rather than a wait-and-see approach raised only after an adverse verdict.
